COMMERCIAL FATLURES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of Commercial Failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending loriday, March 16th, was 186, viz. :—New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 100; Deeds of Arrangement registered, 86. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 109 ; Deeds of Arrangement, 104—total 213 ; being a decrease of 27. The total num- ber of Commercitl Failures recorded during the 11 weeks of the present year is 1,891 ; the total number recorded in the correspondinz 11 weeks of last year was 2,053 showing a decrease of 172.

I have been playing the part of amateur detective, and I flatter myself I have donee rather a good stroke of business, but," and be grew grave again, indeed his lace took a touch of sadness, " I've had enough of the business to last my life. A man who goes in for tracking his fellow creatures ought to have no heart or no conscience, and I'm afraid I possess a little of both." . -e " You are talking Greek,e said Fielding irritably, for the suspense tried him.' " Can't you tell me in plain English whether you have or have not found out the murderer of Dick Blake, alias Norton? " " I can answer you in two words, I have." Joe Fielding kept back his impatience by an effort; he began to understand Sir John meant to tell his story his pwn way. div.head: LATE. MR. H. A. WARING.
div.p: THE LATE. MR. H. A. WARING.
An Indian Tribute.

We have had forwarded to us a copy of the" Madras Mail" for Thursday, February 22nd, which contains the following, contributed by a correspondent : Vallore, 21st February. A heavy gloom has settled on this station owing to the sad death of Mr. H. A. Waring, Principal of the Police Training School, after a lingering illness of fifty days. The deceased was a promising officer of the Police Department, universally popular, respected and loved. His sense of duty was such that while exacting from all his subordinates their portion of duty, he never spardri himself, and set an example of discipline, rectitude and high principle which inspired in the minds of the public an admiration which was spontaneous and genuine. For Ave years as Principal of the Police Training School he was unre- • mitting in his efforts to raise the institution to the high standard it now holds in the estimation of every one of the high officials who have visited it,and who have been lavish in their praises of the man who had identified himself absolutely with the institution which is to be the model for police work in this Presidency. He possessed a very soft heart, and nobody doubted that justice with mercy would be meted out in every case of delinquency. As trustee of St. John's Church, Velloce, the poor had in him a good friend. As a teacher in the Sundayschool he was loved by the children ; and during the absence of the chaplain be read the service in St. John's Church. There was hardly any public function in which he didmot display tha earnestness and !sincerity which characterized his very nature. It will be hard to replace him in Vellore, and sincere and genuine regret andsorrow for his young widow fills the mind of everyone who knew anything of the remarkable personality of " the officer and gentle- man " whose remain4were carrie^) to the cemetery last evening. Mr. Stevenson and the officers of the Train- ing School, with the students, accompanied the funeral cortege, and three volleys were fired over the grave after the service by men of the institution while the "Reveille" was sounded." Most of our readers will recollect that the late Mr. Waring, who was the only con of Captain Waring, of Latchford, died on February 20th. He was married in England last autumn and only returned at the end of October. The illness which terminated so saarra was, we understand, the only one be had had during 'eleven years service in India..

Melbourne firm. I felt certain that the mur- derer was a discarded lover of Miss Jardine and that when he saw her with Norton a mad fit of jealousy took possession of him and caused the crime.

" I felt the clue to the story lay in Australia, but there was not time for me to undertake a voyage to the Antipodes and back, so luckily 1 remembered the cable. lam rich enough to fling, away. a hundred or two without feeling it, and even if my plan failed I should know I had done my best to save my friend. I got from Lady Mary Jardine (it was easy enough to set her talking, poor lady) the name of the Melbourne college where Helen Jardine had been employed before she came in for Alan- dale and learned with surprise that the prin- cipal of St. Monica's was a Miss Murray whose family lived at Thornby for years and whom I had known all my life till she chose to ex- patriate herself. Aliss Murray being an old friend, it was easier to open communication with her than with a stranger. I went to Lon- don and cabled out the bare fact of Alandale's peril, then I went on 'Had Helen Jardine a lover, is he still in Australia, cable back all details.'
"Miss Murray must have a clear head: she saw the drift of my questions without any ex- planation. _ _ .

"Name Charles Gresham, twenty-five, tall, fair, strong, looks like sailor, left for England May by 'Crane,' errand unknown." "You'll think, Fielding, it was not much to go on, but it was sufficient for me. I knew the' Crane' must have arrived some time in June or early July, so I went to the steamer's head office and procured a list of passengers ; sure enough Charles Gresham, of Melbourne, was in the list of those travelling second class. "One of' the stewards of the 'Crane' had left the ship and taken duty on another line of boats which plied between here and America. He happened to be on shore, just back from his first voyage on his new boat. I ran him to earth, and by a heavy bribe got him to tell me all he remembered of Charles Gresham.

" It seemed the ' Crane' had i;;Passengers on that particular voyage, and so Jenkins (that was the steward's name) had no diffi- culty in recalling them. He told me Charles Gresham drank heavily most of the voyage; he seemed like a man labouring under some terrible disappointment or anxiety; some- times he would be in the gayest, maddest spirits, at others A. prey to the most abject despair. " The steward seems to have had a good deal to do with Gresham when he was ill from the effects of drink, and the man talked to him frankly enough. He was a sailor, but the girl he was engaged to had come in for a for- tune and he was going to England to find her or shoot anyone who tried to part them. , Jenkins told me that Mr. Gresham was in that , state of morbid depression brought on by drink, when they got to Tilbury, that the doctor thought him unfit to look, after himself , and tried to find out if he had no friends or relations in England who could be warned of his condition, but Gresham took umbrage and told the doctor to mind his own business."

Joe Fielding had listened with rapt atten- tion, now he broke in with— " Gresham's the man of course, but how in the world did he get away from the .village after the murder without being tracked ? " "I can't tell you that, but I went about asking questions and trying to find out the truth till I found a woman who told me a gentleman had engaged two rooms in her cottage two days before the murder; he had said he might want them for a Week or longer and seemed very free with his money. But she found out he drank and being nervous she took it into her head he might set the house on fire, so she offered him back the rent he had paid in advance and asked him to go else-- where, _ . .

"He took her request 'very nicely,' she said told her to keep the money and he'd go somewhere where they wouldn't be afraid of a poor chap in trouble. He left the cottage the evening of the murder and walked to Thornby Station, where he left his portmanteau in the cloak-room. It was never reclaimed, but the railway officials were too dense to connect that abandoned luggage with the crime with which the whole neighbourhood was ringing. " I had the description of this fellow Gresham imprinted on my brain. I believe I ti-ought so much of the matter that I should have known him if I had met him by accident in the street, but after all I came across him in the -strangest, most unexpected manner. "A favourite servant of my mother's has married and set up a small lodging-house in London, and now and again, perhaps once in a few years,l drop in to see the woman when I an in London. My mother thought highly of her and she was nurse to my poor little sister who aied, so we never look on her as an ordinary servant. "Well, yesterday being in London with a spare half hour I looked in at Mrs. Jonson's and found her in great trouble. One of her lodgers was dying in the house, and the other inmates had fled at the bare whisper of calamity. Too humane to turn the poor fellow adrift, but utterly ignorant of his hiends or relations, the poor woman had nursed him faithfully ; now the doctor declared his hours were numbered and every penny he possessed had been spent for his, l:kenefit ; .he was pounds in Mrs. Jonson's debt and she was dreading the expenses of the funeral. .

" He conies from Australia, sir, and his mother is a widow, that's all I know, the poor woman said to me. 'His name's Gresham, but if I sent a letter addressed Mrs. trreshain, Australia, she would never get it, and he won't tell me where she lives; he says lie's made such a tangle of his life that the sooner he's dead and forgotten the better.'"

div.head: CHAPTER XXI.
div.p: CHAPTER XXI.
JOE FIELDING gave] a sigh of intense relief. " Of course you saw the man—and it was Norton's murderer? "

'! I saw,him ; I told hini I lived near Thorn- by, and asked him if he knew that part of Yorkshire and Alanciale Hall, He gave one look into my face and muttered : 'Tracked down—tracked down! I thought death would have been quick enough to cheat the gallows I ' "Well, Fielding, the long and the short of it is he poured out his story to me and he signed a confession sufficient (I should think) to clear poor Alandale from the faintest breath of suspicion, but I, Call me a fool if you like, I simply couldn't use the confession while he lived; and, you see,) he was dying, poor chap, and I really think fate had been hard on him. I promised he should see Helen Jardine before the end." Joe "gelding stared at the young baronet in unmitigated surprise. I , " ' You promised that—what on earth for ?" he demanded. "Whit good an it do ? " " I don' f know," said Sir John with a shame- faced air as though he expected to be laughed at for the touch of romance in his nature which had made him give the promise. " But life!s been awfully hard on the poor chap, and if one sight of that girl makes death easier to him, by George he shall have it."
" You evidently blame Miss Jardine," sug- gested the lawygr. .
!' I don't know whom to blamei Perhaps,
poor fellow, h was too persister.t and -worried her into the enrrarrement, or she may have
written to break it off and honestly lielieved . .
herself free of him, still it remainS' that his
love for her has spoilt his life and the least she can do is to let him see her before he goes." " But will there be time ? It's a long journey to London, and you said the man's hours were numbered."

"So they are, but he's not in London. I brought him down by the first train this morning; he had an invalid carriage. Mrs. Jenson came to look after him, and he's in- stalled in one of the spare rooms at Leigh Court."

'You brought him there to die, a mur- derer? " Joe did not like the idea. ." I brought him there to die. Rememter he never meant to kill Norton, he yielded to an overwhelming temptation when he saw Helen Jardine meet the man in the darkness of the night ; he could not catch a glimpse of her face, but he had heard the rumour that the heiress of Alandale stole out by night to meet a lover and he was on the watch., " He told me he had laughed„ the rumour to scorn, but when he saw the truth it was too much for him; he was out of his mind for the time being—he watched the girl out of sight and then he fired."

" I don't like Helen Jardine," said Fielding " because she is so strange and secre- tive, but. Sir John, I'm pretty Sure of this, that Lord Alandale loves her dearly ; for his sake ought we, not to prevent this meeting be- tween her and—a murderer ? " " I'll answer for Alandale," said Sir John frankly ; " he'll understand, if he loves his cousin, that the other man's love gives him a right to the boon he craves. As for scandal, there need be none; my aunt' is still my guest, and it can be supposed that the young lady's visit is to her."

" I have come to you from .Sir John Leigh," said Mr. Fielding gravely. "It is believed that we are On the track of the real murderer ; we hdve every hope that by this time to- morrow Lord Alanclale's innocence may be known far and wide. Sir John begs you to pay a brief visit to Leigh Court ; he will not detain you many minutes, and his aunt, the ,Duchess of Quest, is there, so there cam be no gossip about your calling at -a bachelor's house. Sir John bade me tell you it was a matter of life and death and that your cousin, if consulted, would urge you to pat the visit." "I will go," said Helen simply. " You are Lord Alandale's friend, and though you have never been able to like me I will trust you for his sake." ". I have a fly there," said Mr. Fielding; "'there will be no occasion to mention your visit to Lady Mary or Miss Magdalen, unless, indeed, you would prefer to do so." "Oh, no; they will 4iot miss me. Aunt mary and Magdalen are sufficient for each bther. lam only an outsider." There was a pitiful note of , sadness in her last words, but Joe Fielding Was not touched. He thought of the life ebbing fast at Leigh Court, the life which but for this girl's false- ness might lia:ve been long and honoured, and when he remembered Charles Gresham's crime and thought of the sin-laden soul setting out to meet its Judge, he found it hard to be gentle and compasiionate to Helen Jardine. As she passed through the great hall the butler stepped forward and presented a letter just arrived bv no4t to his young mistress. . _ .

• " Lady Mary thought had better give this • to you, Miss Jardine, in case you could send it on:" Helen hardly took in the sense of his words; she imagined the letter to be for herself, but she could spare no attention to it now, and as she slipped it hurriedly into her pocket she did not/even notice the direction or that it bore a foreign stamp. It was not a long drive to Leigh Court and (to Mr. Fielding's relief) Helen did not break the silence by a single question. Things had ,zorne to that pass with her she would have sold her Very soul to purchase Kenneth's ac- quittal, and she did not even trouble to ask herself what Sir John wanted of her; she would have done anything, anything in the world, if tOld it was necessary for her cousin's safety. Sir John met them in the hall, the butler who stood there too at a hint from his master withdrew, so thete \las no one but Mr. Field- ing to hear Sir John's greeting to Helen. " Thank you for Coming, Miss Jardine, I had pledged my word to a dying man that you would do so." Helen started. "A dying man ! " Sir John had given her his arm and led her up the broad open stairs down a long long, passage to a door which he flung open wide for her to enter, then the young baronet turned to Helen. " Forgive me if this comes as a shock' to you. The man who lies here dying has with his last strength cleared your • cousin, Alan- dale's, name from' the least shadow of sus- picion, in return he asks but one boon, that he might see your face before the end." Sir John released Helen's hand and left her to advance alone towards the bed while he retreated from the room, closing the door behind him. Then he stood like a sentinel outside, keeping guard so that no one should interrupt the privacy of that last farewell. ' Hardly knowing what she said, Helen ad- vanced to the bed and looked earnestly on the pale face of the dying man. She had seen Charles Gresham last in the pride of his youth and strength, when his face had the rugged glow of health and his whole conliplexion the fresh tint which cOmes from a life spent in the, open air. For a moment she hardly recog- nised him, but the dying man seized on her with the fitful strength which comes some- times when death is near and in a hollow voice asked : "Where Is Nell ? Why have you come in- stead of Nell ? They Fromised I should see her once before—before I went away." And the woman before him forgot her own secret and her terrible 'dread of its discovery in her pity for Charles Gresham and her long- ing to comfort him. By her own deep hopeless love for Alandale she seemed to realise a little what Charles Grcsham's passion for. Nell had meant to him. Nell could itot come," she said very thoughtfully, " she is no here. Charlie, you will see her very soon again for—" Her sentence was never finished. Gresham had caught her meaning only too well, he clasped his Nra,Aed hands and murmured : —" Nell is gone before. I shall be with her soon." And even as the last words left his lips a strange change passed over his face, a peace unknown to it for years rested on his brow. Charles Gresham was not—for God had taken him. Taken him for what ! For joy or sorrow? Would he be called upon to answer before the great white throne for the life so cruelly, passionately taken ? Or would it be that his late repentance, his last attempt, at atonement, had blotted out the sin?
. . The woman who knelt by his bedside weep- ing, herself a sinner, believed firmly that Charles Gresham's crime was surely par- doned, that as he had " insr.d much" much would be forgiven to him.

t It seemed to Helen in those first dread moments when she found herself alone with the dead that really she, and not poor Charles, had murdered Dick Norton, the crime having been committed through a mistake, because the murderer thought it was his own sweet- heart who met the scoundrel Norton by night. But for the theft of the dead friend's name and position Charles Giesham might never have stained his soul with murder.
CHAPTER XXII.. SOMEONE came in presently and saw what had happened, a woman of middle age with a kind, motherly face. Mrs. Janson kit dread- . . .

fully sorry for the young lady who had been summoned in such haste to say a last good- bye. The good woman went up to Miss Jar- dine and put one hand upon her shoulder. "This is no place for you now, missie, let me take you somewhere where you can rest s. quietly before you go home." "I can't see anyone," said Helen in a ch../ heavy voice, "and I'd rather ,;o home." • j "You must rest a little first," said the kiadly woman, as she led the way to a pretty ' sitting-room opposite the chamber of death. " I'll bring you in :some tea myself and if •you just rest on that sofa a bit, I'll see the carriage I comes round for you in half an hour." " I—l

"L came in a fly," said Helen. think it waited." She was feeling so desperately ill that when Mrs. Jonson disappeared in search of the tea she was thankful to sink down on the sofa; her knees were trembling under her, she felt near to fainting. How much had Charles Gresham told Sir John? She would have given a great deal to know. Anyway, this much was clear, only the poor fellow's death had saved her frorr2; a full exposure of her sin. He was so very near .the • end that, when he saw his/ sweetheart's iriend

" Will you go back to Alandale and fetch instead of herself, he had been past asking Miss Jardine—or shall I ? " questions, past reasoning ; if he had been %but would rather that you undertook the a little stronger, he would have wanted tc task. Remember, Fielding, I am almost a know how Nell could be dead when only the stranger to her." day before Sir John had promised he should Joe Fielding, did not .like his errand. He see her. reached Alatidale Hall a full hour after Helen No, Helen had- been saved by the merest had returned to it, 'but she was still in her chance from discovery, just as a little earlier walking dress when he was ushered into her in the day she had been saved by Mr. Fielding's boudoir, and Joe marvelled if her grief and sudden entrance from the confession of lies anxiety had made her forgetful of the course fraud. . of time. How beautiful she looked, and oh ! "It looks as though I were meant to keep how sad ! j the secret," she told herself ; " an:d now, with Even the commonplace, matter-of-flct Richard dead and Charles Gresham gone too, lawyer felt sorry for the hunted look on het surely, surely lam safe 'from detection. Miss lovely face he did not like Helen Jardine, but Murray is never likely to return to England, seeing her now in her distress he told himself and there is no one else who can prove that I there might be exbuses for her after all ; any am not Helen Jardine. Of course, there's the way it was not his place to judge her harshly. I wrong to Magdalen, she is the rightful heiress, "Is there—is there bad news? " she asked, but I don't think Magdalen carcs mueh for and her voice had a faint worn-out sound as money, and she always says if Alandale had though she could net bring herself to hope any come to her she should have given it back to news that came to her cduld be aught but bad. Kenneth. If he marries me, it will be his, so

that it seems the same thing in the end. He loves me—he loves me more than life, and now that he will be freed from suspicion,' now that Dick's death has broken •my bonds, surely, surely I have a right to be happy, I can't be bound to dash the cup of happiness from my lips without even tasting it." She had yielded once to a terrible tempta- tion on board the yacht "Stella," she had seized at wealth and rank then not for their own sake, but because she longed to be saved from her husband's pursuit and free for ever from his yoke, now an even more potent desire made her well-nigh powerless in the face of a second temptation. She loved Lord Alandale, loved him with a passlon artd tensity which only women who have sulfere.6 terribly and yearned in their loneliness for lovr can feel. As Kenneth's wife, she believed she might be a happy, aye, and even a good woman; once the rubicon passed and his !iring upon her finger, she would be as true and noble a woman as any dead and gone Jardine; aye, even as her cousin, Magdalen, herself. • There was no eanger—or practically none— even if Charles Gresham had confided in Sir John Leigh and the latter told Lord Alanclak of the engagement between his cousin and the murderer ; even then she might " explain " away a great deal of the story, for seeing how Kenneth loved her he would surely believe her version of the affair rather than that of a murderer. Besides (and this at least was,true) Charles Gresham had no right to speak of Helen Jar- dine as absolutely engaged to As she . . .

had told the story.' to Tier friend, he had pro- pOsed to her again and again,; and though she had told him she did not love • him, he'. per- suaded her at last by sheer persistency.. to "try being engaged to him for a few- moutts," to see if she could not learn to love him. - A movement outside the room, Mrs. Jonson was coming back. Helen forced herself to a sitting posture and tried her hardest not to let her face bttray the agony through which she , was passing. She drank the tea offered her with such kindly thought, but did not touch the delicate cake, she felt as though it would have ,choked her, then she asked Mrs. Jonson if the fly were ready., " I would father go home at, once." she told the good Woman, " with6ut' seeing Sir John and the Duchess. I have had a—a shock, and I want to be quite quiet." , But though Mrs. Jonson would have done nothing Willingly against the Young lady's wishes,•Sir John had heard the fly come round and stood in the hall waiting to take leave ot his reluctant guest. Helen need not have feared ,his reproaching her with her treatment of Charles Gresham, she need not have feared .his alluding in any way to her private affairs, for Sir John was a gentleman in the highest sense, and would not for worlds have annoyed a WOMan beneath his roof however much he despised her. It was impossible for Helen to tell. from his manner how much Charles Gresham had told him. " You are looking very ill," he said/ gentle. " Are you sure you feel fit for the drives adon:•? Would not you like Mrs. Jonson or my aunt' maid to go with you ? " •' I would rather be alone." He handed her into the carriage in perfect silence and stood bareheaded till site hae driven out of sight, then he turned back the house with a heavy sigh. There's something wrong," he tvl.l hia self ; "there's something very wrong indeed : that woman looked as though she had passed through a martyrdom. I hope. I hope with all my heart, there's nothing in the Aory that poor Alandale is in love with his cousin." Maria M'ackenzie was spending the evening . at Leigh Court, , for the Duchess of Quest had taken an enormous fancy to Maria and loved to have her bright outspoken companion- ship ; her Grace was a very imperious woman and rather apt to " be a law unto herself." One or two haughty matrons in the -neigh- bourhood had suggested to the Duchess that she would certainly spoil that young, person and turn her head if she continued to take • such an absurd amount of notice of heri!! • but the Duchess only laughed. " What have you to say against the Mackenzies ? " she asked one meddler rather more persistent .than ,the rest.. "The man 0 made his money himself, that's not a clime, provided he made' it honestly. He has a harsh,- overbearing temper ; well, that often . goes hand in hand with great business ability. . I don't Want to make an intimate. friend ot •hint or his wife—though they are cjuite as 'good as lots of people tme meets in' London— ] but the girl is different : to begin with, she' very handsome, then sac is decidedly aniusing, because you never know what she is going to • sav next, • and her , remarks are always Original ; mark my words, if Miss Mackenzie had been presented at Court and talked about , her ' Poppa ' instead of her 'Pa,' if the old man had made his fortune in New York or Chicago instead of Birmingham, his daughter • would have been a great social success." 1 So the 'Duchess o Quest silenced .Marl'i's I detractors. and contrived to have her at Leigh Court as ni4,h as she wished ami (whili would I have ' seemo* a far more difficult matter) 1 to make her feel perfectly at home there. , 1 Maria was sitting alone in he smallest of

the three drawing-rooms, ViliVIL Sit' join, Leigh came in alter putting Helen intp the carriage; something in her face troubled him. What is the matter, liss Mackenzie No bad news from ltockmount. I hone, "
" Oh, no. I was only thinking, Sir John."'" " What about? You can't think how youi face frightened me just snow, it looked sc trolibli.(l." _

" I was thinking of Miss Jardine. I did not mean to spy upon her, Sir John, but I was at the winnow and could not help seeing her as •:the came down the terrace steps. She looked ,o miserable, that I pitied her." " You did not always pity her." " Yes I did, always, even when I thought cite had done that dreadful thing. I used to te,-1 always--even before the Alandale murder —that Hewn Jardine had a secret and that it was a sad one." "Do you always pity people in trouble? " "I --I think so ; perhaps I shouldn't if thr,y Were very horrid. You see Sir John, r have never had any particular trouble of my own, and so I've time to think about other people's."

Sir John made a strange discovery as he listened to Maria, namely, that she was the dearest little girl in the world, and that he with his ancient name and long descent had fallen hopelessly in love with Peter Macken- zie's daughter. He had suspected it -once or twice before, but to-night he was quite sure. Fi .did not tell her so. A man with a strange sense of the fitness of things, he could not have spoken words of love, he could not have tried to secure his own happiness while that terrible wreck of human passion rested beneath his roof. While the angel of death spread his great wings about the Court, it was no time to ask Maria to be the Court's new mistress.

So all he said was: "Try and put Miss Jardine out of your mind ; I'm afraid there's trouble ahead still for Lord Alandale, but don't let's think of it to-night. At least we have the comfort of knowing his life is safe, and after all our fears of the last few weeks that means much." Helen drove away from Leigh Court with a new difficulty—how was she to explain her absence to Lady Mary and Magdalen ? They would certainly want to hear all about her. visit to the Court; what was she to tell them? This question, however, was soort pushed from .her mind by a more important one, for as she put her hand in her pocket for her handkerchief she felt something else there, and suddenly remembered the letter Which had been given her just as she left home. Letters for her were so very few as to be an event .i.nd she took it out thinking it might divert her thoughts for a few minutes. But as she • glanced at the direction she turned ,deadly white; the terrors of this strange day were not over for her even yet, for the letter was addressed to "Miss Hildred Jasper," and the writing was that of the girl friend from whom she had parted on the deck of the blazing "Cygnet." Had the sea given Lip her dead - (To be continued.)

IN SPITE 0.1, NATURE. We can be anything we like nowadays in ' • spite of Nature, writes " Miranda " in the Lady's Pictorial. If Fashion says we shall be tall, she but speaks arid it is done; if she says We are to have sloping or square shoulders, as the CBSO may be, Nature is nowhere. Of late our imperious mistress has set her face against what we euphemistically call "generous proportions." She does not like stout people, so they are gradually disappearing. It is almost discredit- -able to have a " full " figure now whether you .are a man or a woman. Is it dieting that does it? Certainly not. Is it massage? By no means. I this, then, one of the many mysteries for which Fashion is responsible? Not altogether. Most of us know the little secret. It is a simple one, after all, and the means to this very desirable end is certainly not one of which to be ashamed. Nowadays, it is certainly stupid to have adipose tis3ue making itself conspicuous, when, thanks to the clever corsetiere, it is so easy to look elegant without suffering. GIRL'S SPRING COSTUME. div.head: DINNER TO MR. A. H. CROSFIELD M.P.
div.p: DINNER TO MR. A. H. CROSFIELD M.P.
INTERESTING SPEECH BY THE BOROUGH MEMBER. The Chinese Labour Vote.

Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD M.P., was the guest at a dinner held at the Lion Hotel, on Saturday evening in cele- bration of the recent Liberal triumph. The gathering was a highly enjoyable one and was the occasion of some interesting addresses on the work which faces the Government. Mr. C. E. Parker, president of the Liberal Association presided,and among others preses were Mrs. Parker, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., the Rev. H. and Mrs. Dunnico, Alderman Tinnion, Councillors Evans, Wilkinson, Skelland, and Burton, Mr. and Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes, Councillor and Mrs. Peacock, Mr. and Mrs. E. Osborne, Captain Roberts, Mr. and Mrs. W. Furness, Mr. and Mrs. P. O'Brien, Mr. and Mrs. Winstanley. Mr. and Mrs. P. Peacock. Mr. and Mrs. F. Maginn, Mr. and Mrs. W. Bibl4y, Mr. and Mrs. Haviour, Miss Birchall, and Messrs. T. Barnes, John Upson, Nathan Cook, Joseph Elwell, jun., H, Gray, J, Adams, H. W. Guest, J. Hawthorn, James Critchley, J. Worrall, J. T. Lock, E. England, E. V. Walker, J. Morton, Johnstone, and Joseph Howes, jun. It was a matter of regret that Miss Crosfield was unable to attend. The tables were very tastefully decorated with flowers, red being the predominant colour. After dinner, served by Mr. John Lee,proprietor of the hotel, a number of toasts were honoured. "THE KING AND PARLIAMENT."

In proposing the toast of "The King " the CHAIR- MAN said that apart from party considerations he felt it must be a matter of satisfaction to his Majesty that in tha recent election his subjects took such a keen interest in the questions affecting the government of the country. He did not think he was going beyond the limits of propriety in expressing the opinion that it must also be a great satisfaction to the King that in the election there were returned to Parliament repre- sentatives of all classes and that those who from their lives and associations were closely connected with the workibg-classes figured largely in the House. He thought the present Government was keenly alive to the necessities and the considerations of the poor and needy in the country. The subject of the poverty of the unemployed and what was worse still of the unemployable constituted an anomaly in this country of great prosperity and wealth. He thought it must be a great satisfaction to the King that his loyal citizens of Warrington returned a counsellor to the great senate of the empire in the person of their guest—(applause)—who from his intimate associate with the industry of this realm was able to take an intelligent interest, express an intelligent opinion, and give a wise vote upon the many industrial questions which came before the country. (Applause). The toast was enthusiastically honoured.

div.head: LETTERS OF APOLOGY.
div.p: LETTERS OF APOLOGY.

Mr. C. J. HOLMES expressed his regret at receiving the following telegram :—" So sorry cannot well come, Please make my excuses. Truda Crosfield." Mr. Frank A. Roberts to whom they were so greatly indebted for his generosity with regard to the Liberal Club also wrote apologising for non-attendance and expressing the hope that he would be able to visit Warrington at an early date to make final arrangements respecting the Liberal Club and to see some of his old political friends. Mr. F. R. Roberts wrote rejoicing at Mr. Crosfield's great victory and urging the workers to put forth every effort in order to retain the seat. Alderman Pierpoint and Mr. E. J. Guest were also prevented from attending.
THE TOAST OF THE EVENING. "OUR MEMBER."

In the absence of Alderman Pierpoint, the toast of "Mr. A. H. Crosfield, our Member" was proposed by Councillor JAMES EVANS. He said they were there not I merely to wish success to their Member, but to con- gatulate themselves upon the splendid victory which they won at the last election. (Applause). He believed they had won Warrington to keep it. (Applause.) At any rate, he felt they were not easily going to be set aside. (Applause.) He was extremely glad that War- rington had fallen into line with the other progressive constituencies in the country and, as for the majority, it was one of the proudest moments of his life when he heard the figures. (Applause.) He was sure he was voicing the feelings of the townspeople in wishing Mr. Crosfield a long life of usefulness in the House of Commons. (Applause.) Councillor Evans paid a tribute to the splendid services which Miss Crosfield rendered to the cause of Liberalism during the election and con- tinuing said he was never better satisfied with the prospects of the Liberal party than at present. (Ap- plause.) Ile representative Parliament which had been returned was in every way fitted to voice the needs and aspirations of the nation as a whole. (Applause.) Mr. J. A. J. MORTON supported. He appreciated the victory to its full extent in its more important hearing —that was the opening up of Warrington to Liberal principles, and the departure from the old Conservative interests. They were delighted that Mr. Crosfield had attained that position. The bad repute of the late Government did much to bring about the result, but there was something more in the shape of a great wave of feeling on behalf of the unemployed and the poor which seemed to sweep everything before it. In Mr. Crosfield he thought they had a member who would be specially capable of dealing with questions of that kind in Parliament. They knew that the Labour party and especially the Socialists had had great deal to do with the movement and it was greatly to their credit that the unemployed question had been pushed to such an extent. That, coupled with the great wave of feeling and the aversion to a return to Protection, had resulted in the return of a considerable proportion of Labour members. Mr. Cros- field had as oolleagues in the House a certain section which would co-operate with him in those matters for the welfare of the working-classes and the labouring population generally. They were very sorry that a Labour member with whom they in Warrington were well acquainted—Mr. Henry Broadhurst—had been obliged ro retire owing to ill health. (Hear, hear.) There was a considerable force of Labour members who would. see that these extreme Labour and, as they were sometimes called, Socialist questions were properly dealt with. He trusted that Mr. Crostield would live long to give them useful service in the House of Commons. (Applause). The toast was honoured with extreme cordiality.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD'S REPLY. THE CHINESE LABOUR VOTE.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD'S REPLY. THE CHINESE LABOUR VOTE.

Mr. A. H. CfrossuLD, who was received with cheers, said it was with very sincere pleasure that he rose to respond, more particularly on behalf of his sister, who gave him such great help during the election— (applause)—although at the same time he too felt very deeply the remarks that fell from an old friend of his —Councillor Evans—whom he bad known from boyhood, and he appreciated very much the thoughtful address they had had from Mr. Morton. If he might refer to their remarks at once,it would be in order to divide the questions they had alluded to into two parts. They spoke of the work that lay before the Liberal party, and tyro as he was, new-corner as he was in the House, it was quite sufficient to be there for a very few weeks in order future, and hd et tohr ecesaoirmlruymt that tot that rokwu work wasroof ug efforthto. b As that done in the to realise the entire difference of tone and spirit in that necessaryil ou w oul d beCouncillor Evans said, it was not merely because from a personal view he (Mr. Crostield) had achieved a triumph which was the most signal event in his life, that they had assembled there. It was to celebrate that happy change in public spirit and political opinion in their fine old borough. (Applause.) Councillor Evans had spoken very nicely of their political opponents and he (Mr. Crostield) begged to associate himself entirely with those remarks. He too had the pleasure of claim- ing many friends in the Tory party and if he might give them a little word of advice at the moment it was simply this. "Cheer up." They did not like the result from a party point of view, hut it was a jolly good thing for them. At any rate, if he might speak of the mass of the people—and, in the old phrase, it was the greatest number that they had to consider nowadays what he had said was certainly perfectly true, and every , hour he had spent in the House only convinced him that they were at last
GOING TO GET TO BUSINESS and to put into more thorough practice than they had done hitherto those principles that they .had discussed so long, recognizing the rooted individualism of British

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 24, 19
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 24, 19

people and at the same time the pressing neces- sity for qualifying the extreme consequences of individualism which had driven so many people to an opposite and what perhaps might be considered a some- what unwise extreme. It was perhaps a little premature to look into the future at present. He was sure he was speaking honestly for the party and f)r the Liberal principles that his family had stood for generations,when he said that they should leave the question of the man who was to fight for those principles on behalf of the borough an entirely open question in the future; but at the same time make up their minds that as long as they lived they would stick to those progressive prim- ciples.They would do so knowing that if those principles did involve some sacrifice on the part of the mloorlt3 in the Kingdom they would, through a juster measure of taxation,bringing about a better distribution of wealth in the future, through juster legislation all round independent of what they might call directly economi- cal questions, result in a happier, healthier and better state of things for the whole of the people. (Applause). He earnestly associated himself with all that Councillor Evans had said and, at the same time, so long as it was his privilege to press those questions forward in the House they could depend upon it that he would do his best. (Applause.) He did not know that one needed to try to catch the Speaker's eye on every occasion, because he had already noticed that there were lots of people in the House who were very anxious to do that, and there was a common complaint, which was heard equally from the Labour and Liberal members. that there was a bit too much talking. He hoped they would not think it was because he was afflicted with any measure of stage fright that he had not fired off his maiden effort in that august assembly yet. (Laughter.) The simple fact of the matter was that he did not want to be talking there unless one could do some good by talking. Strangely enough,it happened that on several questions connected with education and the infringe- ment of English trade marks—a subject which of course affected Labour ,'and capital in Warrington as much as anything else—he had been thrown into contact with quite a number of distinguished people during the last 'few weeks. He would not have them think he had been trying to be over-pushful in that direction, but he felt ,that a great deal of useful work could be done quietly at Westminster if one knew what he was talking about, and he certainly knew pomething about trade marks and other trade questions. (Hear. hear.) He had also tried to press forward in a quiet way in several quarters what seemed to him a solution, perhaps not a permanent one but which for the time being, at any rate, would give us a chance of a peaceful and useful settlement of what was certainly the thorniest and most difficult problem the Government bad to tackle, and that was

merit would not let plutocrats or even men on the spot drag them into war here, there and elsewhere, and they would not consider that the interests of plutocracy came before those of the main body of the people.(Applause.) Hewes sure it was because they were a progressive party as a whole that the interests of the people that were being considered were not being considered at the dictates of any branch of the party. He would be sorry if it was only by pressure put on that that-genuine Liberal policy was to be pursued. He felt that was not so, and that the co-operation which Mr. Morton alluded to was a very real thing in the House. There was a friendly feeling and A GENUINE CO-OPERATION

..... that was going to do a grand work—the co-operation baiween the Liberal and the Labour parties. They did not want any menace from Liberals to Labour or from Labour to Liberals. If they had to carry through all the work that lay before them there would have to be honest co-operation. (Applause.) So far AS he was concerned, though one had to do one's best to serve the interests of 11 great constituency like Warrington, he naturally felt that his first duty lay with the great mass of the artizans of the town by whose will and pleasure alone he could sit in Parliament. Reference had been made' to the fact that having won a great victory they should maintain their position. He felt that in Warrington, considering the strength not of all the brewers but of the main brewing influence, not of all the clergy of the Established Church but still of the main body of the parsons, considering the strong influences which they did not disguise and which the Progressives had had to face they had, thanks to the united and hearty yet good humoured efforts of both the ladies and men of their party,stormed andiwon one of the strongest Tory citadels in England, and he did not hesitate to tell them so in the House of Commons. (Applause.) It would there- fore be for them to profit by the wisdom of the older men who had been their leaders, of the men of middle age and commercial experience who had done so much for their party, and also by the help of the younger men of new blood who were coming in to strengthen their personnel and the fortifications of the Progressive citadel, so that he would have the duty in future of carrying out work in the House of Commons on behalf of the great num- ber of people in Warrington, having a strong personnel and a really efficient party to back him up. (Loud Applause).
the leaders did their part every man and woman in their organization worked splendidly. (Applause.)
MR. EPSON AND TEIE VICTORY.

Mr. HesoN moved a vote of thanks to the committee and artistes. Tie considered that the real cause of the great victories throughout the country was that they had reverted to the Liberalism of the Gladstonian period. The English people were sick of shilly-shally- ing, of the tampering with principle, of the pandering to vested interests, and of the lowering of the standard of national life, and although there had been in our history some reversions almost to barbarism when the British people had been almost staggering to its doom with its hands full of blood,vet essentially the heart of England was sound, moral aril righteous. it had been because of the tam- pering and the trifling with matters of principle that the English people said " We will have this Ro longer, but we will again stand by those principles of righteousness, justice and liberty which have made us great and famous in the days that are past." The election had been to many of them a most comforting assurance that the people of England were not on the moral downgrade which some of them had feared they had begun to descend. (Applause). During the evening a very enjoyable musical pro- gramme was submitted. Miss E. Birchall and Mr. Cook very creditably interpreted several songs and violin and pianoforte duets were cleverly executed by Mrs. Haviour and Mrs. Holmes. A pianoforte solo by Mrs. Holmes, who also acted as accompanist. was much appreciated. A humorous song by Mr. P. ITignett proved a popular item.

div.head: QUESTION OF EDUCATION.
div.p: THE QUESTION OF EDUCATION.

_ . Perhaps they would think he was taking too much upon himself in making those remarks. He did not pretend to be an expert on education, but he had had the advan- tage of hearing the views of those, he thought, who were chiefly responsible for the settlement of the question, and he need not tell them that that in itself had already been a great education There were people who were returned to the House who had given the whole of their lives to politics and who were almost qualified teachers when they went there, but he at any rate was in the very opposite position. Most of those present followed politics from the point of view of broad principles. They had their businesses, and during the last twenty-two years he personally had had as big a business strain upon him probably as any- one in that room. He had lightened that strain of late years. He had to do so or he could never have occupied the position he was in now. Still, business heretofore had been the chief and first claim on his thoughts, energies and responsibilities. It was now the second claim,and he hoped they would bear him out that he was therefore carrying out the promise he made before the election that if he was elected for Warrington, though he could net afford to entirely sever himself from commercial undertakings, they would certainly take a back seat and the chief responsibility on his shoulders an long as he represented Warrington would be the political responsibility. He did not know whether he ought to cry peccavi or make any allusion to short comings that had already occurred. He thought be would just on that one occasion. When he had the privilege of speaking on other occasions in Warrington, however,he did'not intend for a moment to waste time on

PUERILE PERSONALITIES that would be very much better devoted to discussing measures which they had before them. But, to slightly alter the old saying, " Fierce is the light that beats upon the politician,"and be awoke one morning to read in two columns of a certain paper that he had withheld his support from the Government on the question of all others that he would like to give it the strongest possible backing. He was really sorry to detain them with these little details, but it was the last time he would do it. He had, explained Mr. Crostleld, hoped greatly to have the privilege of address- ing a newly-formed organization in Warrington association that was giving more power to their political elbow, and which was destined to do good and great service, along with other organizations in the town—he meant the Junior Liberal Association. In order to be able to do so he went to the PWhip and did his best to get a pair, and he could tell them it was not very easy to get one now-a-days, because if they paired very many of those good gentlemen on the other side they would wipe them out altogether. (Laughter). However, he succeeded in getting one, and counted on coming down to Warrington, but then he committed a very great sin because he got laid up with catarrh and a touch of ncuralgia which pulled him down very severely and be was unable to leave the house at all.He explained that in answer to some good friend of theirs in War- rington who signed himself" Voter "and. who seemed to be very anxious. He also explained the circumstances a second time in another letter, and yet this critic of theirs said he ventured to doubt whether he (Mr. Crosfleld) had a pair at all,and whether he did not withhold his support from the Government on that enormously important question of Chinese labour. If the writer to whom he was alluding could not accept his statement, deliberately made on two occasions, he would perhaps excuse him (Mr. Crostleld) from discuss- ing that or perhaps any other question with him in future. The introduction of the Chinese into South Africa was a serious matter. He could assure them he had discussed it with men on both sides—with men who were largely interested in the employment of _ _

CHINESE Lattourt as well as with men on the Liberal side who held as firmly as he (Mr. Crosfleld) hold that the introduction' was absolutely unnecessary—(applause)—had labour out there in the first instance and all along been treated Drop 3rly, and as labour would have to be treated if it Were in England which, after all, like the Transvaal, was under the British flag. Continuing, Mr. Crosfield said that Mr. Morton seemed a little doubtful as to whether the Government was really going to get to businev. He (Mr. Crosfleld) would like to point out that he did not suppose there were a hundred men in the House of Commons who knew all the " in and outs" of procedure. It took a long time before one got what Frenchmen called au courant with most of the procedure there. He would not venture to criticise the system, because he did not know how far time might be saved or how far it would be inadvisable, but he Wi`c; certain that, allowing for the question of pro- cedure and for what was very much more serious—the danger of emasculation of work in the House of Lords —the House of Commons absolutelyimeant business. He thought the House, after all, was a reficztion of opinion in the country. He had been in the country and talked to very advanced Radicals with whom he associated himself, but if they talked even with people who were a little bit more timid they would find a great change now. To talk about

div.head: TAXING LAND
div.p: TAXING LAND

a few years ago was like laying one's hand on the Ark of the ConYenant—it was sacrilege. The same applied to graduation of income tax which he had always looked upon as a just and splendid source of revenue if pro- perly carried out. To graduate the tax up to 10 per cent, was the proposal at present, but if he was not mis- taken it would in future be graduated to more than 10 per cent, on people with enormous incomes, hut it would be arranged carefully and wisely in such a way as not to restrict the legitimate ambition and the energy of a man who WP9 trying to build up a little or a largo fortune for himself, loose proposals were looked upon as revolution not very long since, but it was not so now. He had heard those propositions pass without one word of adverse criticism. He did not know what had come over their friends of the Opposition. Perhaps they had scarcely a kick left in them—(laughter)—but they sat silent and heard those proposals which were going to reform taxation enormously and which he must say to his mind were even more important than the very strong opinions that one heard expressed in the House in favour of more economy. Of course, they all subscribed to the necessity for economy where it could be practised, and there was no doubt that under the last Government a great deal of shock- ing waste occurred. But when all was said and done, if a proper programme was to be carried out in order to I better the condition of the r3ople as a whole and to improve the conditions of life of England, in a great ' many cases it meant money, and he did not think it would be any use talking about it unless they were pre- I pared to face what was called the tapping of FRESH SOURCES OF TAXATION. It was .no use talking about giving old age pensions— on which there was certainly a pretty general agreement amongst the enormous majority of the House,—unless they were prepared to go in for the fresh taxation to raise the funds. We had enough money to give old age pensions if the late Government had avoided that one, single, wasteful, disastrous war in South Africa, but it was not good enough to say that because that huge and criminal blunder was committed we had not got the money to do this, that or the other in the way of social legisla- tion. The money would be found quickly enough if we had to face another big war and we could find money for better purposes than that. (Applause.) That led up to another point which seemed to mark one great dividing line between the truly democratic Parliament which they now had at Westminster and the mere Government of cliques and vested interests which pre- ceded it. The difference was as widely separated as the poles and they shw it in the whole of the Govern- ment's South African policy as it had been laid down so far in the most important speeches deliveredk Lord Loreburn, the Lord Chancellor, Mr. Asquith, Ind Mr. Winston Churchill. They saw it distinctly laid down that what to his mind was one of the worst features of the last Parliament, perhaps the very worst—the ( worship of plutocracy—was put an end to. The Govern-

div.head: LIBERAL PARTY.
div.p: THE LIBERAL PARTY.

This toast was proposed by Alderman TINNION who commented upon the healthy and vigorous state of all the local party organizations. Probably the one thing which had contributed more than anything else to the prcfsent position of Liberalism in the town was the absolute disgust of all people of progressive ideas with the conduct of the late Government. Another impor- tant point was that all sections of the party took the opportunity of sinking minor differences and worked with one common object —to overthrow the Conservative Government and to return in its place a Government of which everyone of them was proud. (Applause.) Alder- man Tinnion expressed regret that he had felt obliged to relinquish the chairmanship of thp Executive Com- mittee, but said the position wouldle very ably filled by Councillor Evans. He felt sure that the same spirit which had animated the party for some years would continue and that they were all determined to have real progress with good legislation, not for the favoured few but for the many. (Applause.) Mr. EDMUND OSBORNE supported and alluded specially to the work of the Junior Liberal Association, which, he said, was composed principally of young men of Progressive, Liberal views who were determined to acquire a fuller knowledge of politics, not to be tied down to any particular line of action, but to think for themselves and set an example in progressive ideals. They had excellent debates on social and political topics which had enlightened them to a very great extent as to the ideals which they should emulate. He was very sorry Alderman Tinnion had been compelled to relinguish the chairmanship of the Executive Committee because he was satisfied that the way he had conducted the affairs of the Association would be of value to him (Mr. Osborne) in the duties of the secretaryship which he hoped to undertake. He was, however, satisfied that the alderman would have a capable successor in Coun- cillor Evans. There was a great hope for the future. They had won a decisive battle ; they were not afraid; and they intended to do their utmost to maintain their position. (Applause). Councillor WILKINSON responded and also spoke of the healthy state of their organizations. He expressed the hope that the leaders of the party would visit the Liberal Club more frequently.

div.head: LADIES. MRS. PARKER AND THE SUFFRAGE QUESTION.
div.p: THE LADIES. MRS. PARKER AND THE SUFFRAGE QUESTION.

Mr. H. W. GUEST proposed the toast of "The Ladies" and referred to the great wave of feeling which was sweeping over the country in favour of women's politi- cal rights. He felt that the women who were called upon to pay taxes and bear other responsibilities equally with men should be entitled to exercise the Parliamen- tary vote. Mrs. PARKER responded. She expressed regret at the absence of Miss Crosfield whose energy during the election campaign was an inspiration to them all. She thought the women did very well during the election —(hear, hear)—and their services were very willingly given. She hoped that as they had got so much fresh zeal and life in the Association they would continue to do a quiet, steady profitable work. It would be a good thing if they could hold meetings regularly for instruc- tion. It might not be ganerally known that a branch of the Association which was educating public opinion in favour of Woman's Suffrage had been formed in Warrington. There was no thought of women becom- ing Parliamentary representatives and there was no wish at present that all women should have the vote. They only desired that those who possessed the qualifications should not he debarred by sex from exercising the franchise. The women Liberals generally and those who were interested in the subject deplored far more than any men could do, the fact that there were women who had conducted themselves in such an unwomanly way as some of the suffragists had done in other towns during the election. They gained nothing by it. but rather tended to put back the cause twenty or thirty years. She thought all who studied the question seriously and intelligently would come to the con- clusion that the granting of the vote to those women who were qualified would be a helpful measure.(Applause)

div.head: CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN.

Mr. C. J. HOLMES proposed the toast of" The Chair- man " and said Mr. Parker had been a tower of strength to the party in the arduous and memorable contest they had gone through. There was no question that his retaining of the presidency would help to keep the party in a strong position, and enable them to continue to look upon Warrington as a Liberal borough. (Applause.) The Rev. H. HUNNICO supported, and said be believed it was largely due to Mr. Parker's admirable leadership that they were able to capture the seat. A great num- ber of factors helped them. There was the discreditable record of the late' Government which had plunged the country into a disastrous war, introdUced an un-English 1 form of labour into South Africa, and thrown our educa- tional system into chaos. They had threatened to tamper with the foundation upon which we had built our commercial supremacy and he thought all these things tended to win the election for Liberalism. It seemed to him that the other day the Prime Minister put into words what the English people put into action at the election when he said "Enough of this foolery. Let us I get to business." (Applause.) Locally a great number of things helped them. They were well led by their leaders, well organized by their election agent, and the rank and file followed splendidly. The one point he I would like to emphasis c was that the victory in War- rington was a democratic victory. (Applause.) He had no hesitation in saying that if the party kept united and thoroughly democratic they would be able to retain quite as easily the seat which they won gloriously at the last election. (Applause.) Mr. PARKER in responding, said Mr. Holmes bad retired from the secretaryship of the Association and he (Mr. Parker) would like to voice in the name of that gathering their appreciation of the good work he had done for the Associntion for so many years. Their best wishes went with him in his retirement from active work. Mr. Parker expressed his willingness to visit the Liberal Club more frequently if the members desired it,and said he considered the Club one of the strongest points in their organization. As Mr. Dunnico remarked the recent electionwas a democratic victory for although

div.head: BAD TEETH AND DIGESTION.
div.p: BAD TEETH AND DIGESTION.
Nottingham Man Describes His Relief from Indigestion and Biliousness by Mother Seigel's Syrup.

Of the many evils that beset modern life, few have worse results than the early loss of teeth. " All ,my troubles arose from bad teeth," says Mr. Thomas I Rawson, proprietor of the Prince Leopold Hotel, Moffatt-street, St. Anne's Well road, Nottingham, in a letter to the proprietors of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, dated August 16th, 1905. " My teeth failed me very early in life," continues Mr. Rawson, " and I had the utmost difficulty in chewing my food, being obliged to nibble like a rabbit, as one may say. "Of course, my digestive powers broke down under these unnatural conditions. At first pain and wind resulted from everything I ate, but it was not long before I was always in pain; eating or fasting, I could not escape it. Often headache,accornpanied by a drowsy feeling, which I was quite unable to overcome, com- pletely unfitted ma for work. Thus I continued going from bad to worse, until at length my stomach became incapable of. retaining food at all ; it was rejected almost immediately it was swallowed. For some time I subsisted upon hot milk, being absolutely afraid to partake of anything more substantial. Poor diet for a man busily engaged all day ! As I grew weaker, an additional trouble befel me—nothing less than rheuma- tism in my feet and legs—and my condition became that of a confirmed invalid. "For two years I was attended by a doctor but his utmost skill did no more than occasionally relieve me, and at the end of that time I seemed as far from being cured as ever. It was the same with various patent medicines recommended to me, until I tried Mother Seigel's Syrup. Then my health began to mend. Soon could relish and retain food, eating was not followed by pain, and rheumatism ceased to trouble me. At present my health is good, with every prospect of remaining so, though I still occasionally take a dose of the Syrup."

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
THE ONLY " ZERMANENT " GAS.

Writing in the Athencrum on helium and the transmutations of elements, Sir William Ramsay tells us that helium is to be detected by its spec- trum in many of the fixed stare, nctably Capella, Arcturus, Pollux, Sirius, and Vega. It is one of the lightest of gases, being only twice as heavy as hydrogen; but unlike hydrogen, however, its molecules consist of single atoms, whereas those of hydrogen consist of paired atoms, which separate only when hydrogen en- ters into combination with oxygen or other ele- ments. This peculiarity appears to render liquefaction of helium almoq impossible; for while hydrogen has been liquefied, and boils at 422 deg. Fahr. below zero, helium has been cooled to —438 deg. Fahr.. and has been com- pressed to one-sixtieth of it ordinary bulk, and yet has shewn no sign of liquefaction. Indeed, it is now the only " permanent " gas, for it has never been condensed into liquid form. The minerals which contain helium have one thing in common: they all contain uranium or thorium or lead, or a mixture of these. Minerals of lead alone do not shew the presence of helium; but it may be stated ,that helium is an invariable constituent of ores of uranium and thorium. It was at first supposed that such minerals contain helium in a state of combina- tion; but this view oould not be substantiated, for the constituents of these ores do not chew any tendency towards combination with helium.

div.head: SNAKE POISON.
div.p: SNAKE POISON.

So far as is known, snake poison consists of a peptone, which produces ulceration, an unknown virulent substance which causes infiltration of blood when injected into the tissues, and an al- bumen wbich is not, apparently, poisonous. Now, when snake venom is concentrated by re- moving the third substance and retaining the other two, what is left constitutes the most powerful poison know to toxicology. It is forty times more powerful than the original snake venom. It has been reckoned that a single thimbleful of it, su'i.k,ablv applied, would be enough to kill 25,000 people.

div.head: MILLIONS AND MOSQUITOES.
div.p: MILLIONS AND MOSQUITOES.

Some interesting experiments, writes a corre- spondent, are being conducted in several of the British Colonial possessions in the West Indies, for the purpose of aseertaining how far the im- munity enjoyed by Barbados from the visitations of the malarial mosquito is due to the presence in the local waters of a tiny fish known as "millions." As far back as the year 1888, speci- mens of the Trinidad variety of this little fish were determined by the authorities at South Kensington, its habits being similar in every re- spect to the Barbados species. Its voracity is out or all proportion to its size, and as its food con- sists to a large eitent of the larvte of the mos- quito it cannot be doubted that its operations constitute a very' potent factor in rendering the rrea in which it lives free from malarial fever. Places which have long been known to be the recognised breeding haunts of mosquitoes have become quite harmless after the introduction of these fish. It is believed that a far more effec- tual method of eradicating the mosquito is to be found in inducing them to lax their eggs in re- ceptacles to which the " millions " have been pre- viously . introduced, than to rely solely on kerosene or petroleum, although the last-named Would seem to be peculiarly suitable for dealing with the stagnant water which collects in the gutters of large buildings and is a favourite haunt of the militant mosquito.

div.head: POISON IN BEES' EGGS.
div.p: POISON IN BEES' EGGS.

M. C. Phisalix is well known for his re- sr•arches on snake and other poisons. In the case of the toad and viper he has shewn that the specific poison accumulates in the ova, and sug- gests that it plays an important part in develop- ment and inheritance. His latest studies relate to the poison of the bee's sting. Bees' eggs, he shews, contain minute qua.ntities 4if the poison, 475 eggs being required to furnish enough to poison a sparrow.
A REMARKABLE METEORITE. What is described as the largest, strangest, and by far the most interesting meteorite in the world has come into the possession of the Ameri-

can Museum of Natural 'History. This stray bit of some faraway planet is known as the Willa- mette Meteorite, and was discovered by two prospectors named Hughes and Dale in the woods of Willamette county. This great meteorite, says thb New York Times, is in the form of an abbreviated cone, having its base on two sides so prolonged as to produce an oval who long diameter is one-third greater than its transverse diameter. There are no angular outlines to the mass as a whole; all, whether in vertical or horirontel sections, are bounded by broad curves. In the lower half of this great cone are a number of ROUND BORE - ROLES,

irregular as to position and more general near the bottom or base of the meteorite. These holes are nearly circular and well defined. They are from lin. to 4in. in depth and 3M. to Sin, in diameter at the outside. Another feature of this remarkable meteorite consists in the deep furrows or channels cutting into the lower cone area. These furrows extend vertically to the lower edge or base of the mass, whose border they break with channelling. The extreme length of this

The other analysis shews iron. 9165; nickel, 7•88; cobalt. '2l; phostihorus. 'O9. The specific gravity of the iron is 71. The colour of the exterior of the meteorite is a dull reddish brown. The mass is much oxidised. with a ten- dency to scale in small flakes. The fractured sur- face is more coarsely granular in structure than other iron, and is of a formation peculiar to itself.

div.head: PILOT TO HEALTH.
div.p: PILOT TO HEALTH.

A beverage that imparts mental and bodily vigour, and is companuively easy of digestion, may be described as a "pilot to health." Such a beverage is Cadbury's cocoa. It is "staying and bracing," and as it stands by you longer than any other beverage—it is a good " emergency meal." Cocoa is strongest when pure. " Cadbury's is the Standard of highest purity," vide the Lancet. Cadbury's cocoa is therefore strongest. It makes the most dainty and digestible beverage, and is " On nicest cocoa.' \

div.head: RADIUM ANT) CORPUSCLES.
div.p: RADIUM ANT) CORPUSCLES.

Corpuscles, said Professor' J'. J. Thomson at the Royal Institution, speaking on "The Cor- puscular Theory oi Matter," were discovered to be of every-day occurrence, and were given out in large quantities by metals when raised to red heat. A copious stream of corpuscles came from hot lime. They were also given out when metals were exposed to light, especially ultra violet light. There was a theory that the Aurora Borealis was due to the action of corpuscles com- ing from the sun, and striking the tipper regions of the atmosphere. Corpuscles were, in fact, of common occurrence, and could be found in the most unexpected places. Radium gave out cor- puscles at all speeds, and some of them nearly approached the velocity of light.

div.head: NOVEL LIFE-FLOAT.
div.p: A NOVEL LIFE-FLOAT.

A new type of life-raft has been invented in the United States, of which the centre of gravity is so low that it is impossible to upset it. The Scientific American describes it as resembling a huge life preserver, being constructed with a flotation cylinder formed into an oval-shaped ring. A slatted wooden platform is suspended 3it below the, cylinder by means of a rope net- ting. The flotation cylinder consists of a con- tinUous copper tube divided into twelve or thirteen air-tight compartments, according to the size of the float The tube is stiffened by means of longitudinal flanges. To protect the tube it is coated with a non-corrosive paint, and then covered with a layer of compressed cork 2in. thick. i This serves as a buffer for the copper tubes, and also adds to the buoyancy of the raft. The Cork is wrapped with waterproofed cloth, and over this heavy canvas is wound. A final coat of waterproof paint renders the float en- tirely proof against action of the weather or water. The platform or floor of the float is of such size that it will fall through the flotation ring so that no matter how the float strikes the water it will always be right side up. The oc- cupants stand on the platform within the ring. Each float is fitted with oars and painters lashed to the cylinder. This protects them 'from the wash of waves, and prevents them from being snept away. Since about half the load is under water and partially sustained by its own buoy- ancy, the flotaticin cylinders do not have to be as large as do those of the ordinary typo of raft. In fact, the Government has made a special pro- vision for this particular life-float, allowing it a buoyancy of 145•51 b. per capita on the 'ocean, and 1211 b. on lakes. But this float will safely carry even more than its oflidal rated capacity. A larger one measuring about B.lft. by 12ft. over all,\ with cylinder measuring 20in. in diame- ter, has a rated capacity of twenty-three persons on the ocean and 27.7 persons on bass. This type of life-float occupies but little space on a vessel. Owing to their ring-shape, a number of floats of different sizes may be nested together to save stowage space. A aril! more economical arrangement, adapted particularly for private yachts, is to fit the float with buoyant cushion .1.1,4:1011y oesigliCol tor tne purpose, Otis forming a deck divan. The cushion is covered with leather or duck, and a like covering is pro- vided for the cylinder, thus completely disguising the float.

Annual Police Inspection. On Tuesday morning the Warringtan County Borough Police Force was inspected by Lieut. Col. Eden, His Majesty's Inspector of Constabulary for the Northern District. Col. Eden was met at the Central Statioq. at 10.50 a.m. by the Chief Constable and Detective Superintendent Monaghan, who accompanied him to the Police Buildings, where he was met by Mr. Alderman Smethurst (representing the Watch Com- mittee) ; Mr. G. F. F. White, Justices' Clerk; Dr. Smith, Police Surgeon, and other gentlemen. The whole Force, with the exception of a very few men who were on duty in the streets, was drawn up in the Parade Room, where the men's kits and appointments were also set out in military fashion. The Government Inspector at once proceeded to make a minute inspec- tion of the men and their uniform and accoutrements. This concluded the men fell in for drill on the open space adjoining the Police Buildings, where they were put through a number of movements by the Chief Constable and Chief Inspector Phillips, the police drill instructor. At the conclusion of his inspection Col. Eden was more than complimentary in his expressions of satisfaction with the manner in which all members of the Force had acquitted themselves, espeCially at drill. The Inspector WAS also pleased with the condition of the men's kits and accoutrements, while he specially com- mended the new style of summer uniform. The Inspecting Officer next made the usual inspection of the police headquarters,visiting the various offices,store rooms, etc., and also the cells and thg living quarters of the unmarried constables. He again praised the arrangements of the whole and, while inspecting the living quarters, expressed his admiration of the system which, be said, was obviously to be credited with much of the force's high standard of conduct and efficiency. Colonel Eden next devoted attention to the books and records of the force, with the careful, intelligent and accurate keeping of which he was thoroughly satisfied. The Inspector wished his high appreciation of all that he had seen to be conveyed to th. Watch Committee, and instructed the Chief Constable to embody his (Colonel Eden's) remarks in general orders. The Inspector complimented Dr. Smith, police surgeon, on the healthy appearance of the members of the force,and the low rate tzf the year's sickness. He further added that the efficiency of the police matron's work was obvious in the cells and living quarters.
