div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
MARCH 24th 1906.

The legislative portion of MR. LLOYD the Session commenced on GEORGE'S Tuesday with a conspicuous " MAIDEN " BILL, triumph for Mr. LLOYD- GEORGE, whose Bill for the amendment of the Merchant Shipping Acts was received with practically general applause. It is impossible not to recall Mr. CHAMBERLAWS ill- omened attempt to carry a similar measure. More than twenty years since the then President of the Board of Trade in a Liberal Government contrived to rouse up against him every shipowner in the country. He went on a sort of pilgrimage of passion, for the purpose of converting -is opponents but in this he had no success. Then there, were threats of great trade union demonstrations and marches from the Midlands, which never took place. Mr. CDAMBERLATN'E Bil \ bad eventually to be withdrawn, and nobody regretted its disappear- ance. It had been badly drawn and badly engineered. It was brought forward in the spirit of a raging and tearing campaigner, and for that among other reasons, it was the first of its author's great failures. Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE introduced to the House of Commons a moderate and sensible measure in a moderate and sensible way, and found himself loaded with congratulations, and cheered onward with good wishes from members on both sides.

The single discordant note was introduced by Mr. GEORGE WYNDHAM, of whom we should up to this time have been disposed to say that his one great talent is his unfailing tact, it appears,how- ever, that his tact is not unfailing. It failed him on Tuesday. Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE proposes that after the expiration of a three years' notice,foreign vessels trading to English ports shall be placed under the same regulations as British ships. Mr. WyNnnem chose for controversial purposes where no controversy need have arisen, and where it was very much out of place, to hail this as a step on the path to Protection. We ought not, perhaps, to complain of this triviality, seeing that only Mr. WYNDEIAM can suffer by it. The President of the Board of Trade passed it over without notice when he came to reply. There was no other voice raised except voices of approval. The English shipowner has lone felt bitterly aggrieved because foreign vessels trading to the same ports as himself, and often setting off from the same docks and wharves, are free in respect of overloading, seaworthiness, and the carrying of life-saving appliances, from the restrictions to which he is himself compelled to submit. This is the state of thinks which is to be brought to an end three years after the passing of the Bill which was introduced by Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE. Vessels calling at our ports and taking passengers away are to be subject to our cabin passenger regulations. Provision is to be made that no seaman shall be engaged on board British ships unless, like the Lascars, they are British subjects, until they have satisfied a competent officer of the Board of Trade that they can understand orders when they are issued to them in English. This is a condition of things rendered necessary, as the Presideut of the Board of Trad3 remarked, in the interests of the safty of the ship and crew. Then there is to be a standard, or what would prove to be a minimum scale of provisions, to which shipowners will be required to conform. Kr. 14LoYD-Gaonoa males no complaint against shipowners in general.He says that the greet majority of them provide their sea- men with food that is good in quality and ample in quantity, but legislation is necessary to meet the exceptional cases. The more ill-conditioned ship- owners mnst be made to live up to the standard of the majority, said the President of the Board of Trade. Finally, ships' cooks are to be certificated. To be" the sou of a sea cobk "is, in the language of the Mercantile Marine. to be an object of unmitigated contempt. In future the sea cook will be required to know something at least about the grek art of cooking.

The Bill is one which considers the interests alike of shipowners and seamen. It will remove some of the ' chief grievances of both. It will make life in the forecastle tolerable, and it will relieve the British shipowners of the pressure of what is undoubtedly an unfair form of competi- tion. No shipping Bill ever introduced to the House of Commons has had so general and hearty a welcome.

The study of the Chinese QUESTION OF FACT Labour vote in the House AND OF GOOD TASTE of Commons and Mr. Oros- field's part therein has some interesting features which are worth recapitulat- ing. Out readers will remernh,3r that the " Observer " raised quite a big commotion because the Member for Warrington was not in his place m the occasion of this, the first important livision in the House, and condemned him in strong terms for neglecting the interests of his constituents. The following week, Mr. Crosfield very considerately explained the reason for his absence—illness—and mentioned the fact that he had given support to the government by securing a " pair " on this important occasion. On March 10th, the week after, our pertinacious contemporary sneered at the Member's explana- tion, his indisposition, and with regard to his pairing,: ventured to "express a doub:,." This
gt tl co di ir

• was very rude and undignified. We should have thought even Mr. Crosfield's opponents—bitter as they seem to be—would have accepted his word. They have usually been generous enough to con- cede that he was a gentleman. On Saturday last the " Observer" devoted another note to Mr. Crosfield and announced that he had paired on this particular occasion with Mr. S. Roberts, the Conservative member for the Eccleshall Division of Sheffield. Evidently, after having questioned Mr. Crosfield's veracity, they had made inquiries and found that he had really told the truth. We should have thought that common courtesy would have impelled our contemporary to express regret at having doubted the word of a gentle- man—and that gentleman the Member for the Borough—in regard to a public matter. Bat there is no trace of any such generous and fair- minded spirit. The " Observer's " regret seems to be that it has not caught Mr. Crosaeld tripping. This sad lapse from the amenities of public life on the part of our opponents will, we are sure, be deplored and condemned by all right-thinking people in Warrington. Mr. It. Pierpoint always maintained a high standard of courtesy when he upheld the C msarvative banner. We should he loth to think that on his departure from tho representation of the Borouzli, the god inannera of his supporters went with him.

Can elementary day THE COST OF THE Schools, satisfactory to ScEIOOLS. the Board of the Ethica- tion, he built at a cost oughly of £lO per head —i e, £lO 000 for 1,000 children? The question is one to which there was no satisfactory answer after two and a half hours discussion at the special Council meeting on Mon- day. It was not solely to settle such an interest- ing problem that the Council had met, but to confirm or rescind resolutions of the Education Committee, accepting plans and tender for the Bolton school to be built at Latchford. The ques- tion arose out of the business and is, in fact, inseparable from any consideration of it. Briefly, the facts of the matter are these: The Education Committee advertised for plans from architects for the new school, one of the main conditions being pli- that the plans should be drawn on a basis which would bring the cost of the school within 5 per cent. ' of £lO per head—roughly £lO 10i. The architects complied, but few of the plans were deemed to conform with the requirements of the Board of Education. One lot were adopted, however— those of Messrs. Wright, Garnett, and Wright— whose estimate of the cost was £7,424, for 720 scholars, a figure which agreed nicely with the conditions. The builders and the architects, how- ever, seem of erection, to have a different idea as to the coat and no tenders at anything like the stipulated figure were received. The committee seems to have somewhat too readily bowed to what may or may not have been the inevitable, and the tender of Mr. H. Fairclough at £11,418 was accented—a figure which works out at £l5 17s. per head, or an increase of about 50 per cent. The plans were adopted last April, the builder's Contract in February last, and confirmed by the '• Council on March 6th—without, however, any 1 explanation being given as to the enormous dis- • erepancy as regards cost between £lO 10s. and , £l5 17s. per head. This was discovered later by , the economists of the Town Council, and resultedl • in Monday's special meeting. The sequel is that the minutes of the Educatiun Committee referring , to this matter are referred back for further con- , oideration. There is some reason to believe that the Sites and Buildings Sub-Committee hoped for tenders at £lO 10s. per head, but did not expect them. The question now is: Can this school— • On others which have to follow—be built to the conditions laid down ? We think they can, or at , any rate they ought to be, and it is the Education Committee's duty to try, try, try again until it ' gets appreciably nearer the figure which it has oc'en fit to specify. Only this week the Eccles •t ducation Committee has accepted a tender for the erection of a school in Patricroft to accorno- date 1,100 children at £7,687 exclusive of play- ground, heating and lighting. This works out at Under £7 per head. £lO 10s. per head should provide schools which will answer all requirements and at the same time be more presentable to the eye than the "barracks and warehouse tyos instanced in Germany. -- Warrington people ar THE INvraattax shortly to be appealed to ExrEaratots. for generous support on behalf of a particularly deserving undertaking. There is no more useful or highly appreciated institution in the town than , the Infirmary, and great numbers can testify from actual experience to its noble work. Unfortun- ately, the accommodation has of late Droved quite inadequate to cope with the constantly-increasing demands upon it, and the authorities have felt compelled to embark upon a scheme of extension - At the annual meeting of the Governors .. on Thursday. afternoon it was decided to . a motion the Board of Management's proposal for the erection of a pavilion which would contain ' sixty-six beds and bring the total accommodation up to 104, and a separate home for the nursing ' staff. The total cost of this urgently-needed improvement will be from £lO,OOO to £12,000 and , We have sufficient confidence in the generosity of ' the townspeople when appealed to on behalf of 1 such a splendid cause to believe that the amount i. Will be raised. Mr. William Long, J.P., has set ', an excellent example by forwarding the handsome , donation of £l,OOO and with such a start the fund ' Mould speedily attain substantial proportions. The Hon. Misses Wilson-Patten have showu their continued interest in the town by sub- ocribing MO and we feel sure the scheme has only to he brought clearly before the com- tounity to call forth a hearty response from all a_uarters. It was pointed out at the meeting that Warrington occupies a low place among the towns of the country in regard to the extent of its voluntary hospital efforts and we trust that ere long this reproach will be removed and that War- rington will have an Infirmary in every way corn-. rnensurate with the growing needs and the imiportance of the borough.

-- Co-incident with the quick- A GOVERNMENT cued sod improved public OF "NON-TRAnxits." spirit in Warrington it is gratifying to find that the riW Government sets an admirable example of 'public service without personal pecuniary profit. 'Ou taking office, all the members of the new Administration who held directorships of public "Panies resigned those directorships—a course Which the members of the late Government did y not see fit to take. Mr. Claude Hay put pies. tioos to the Prime Minister in respect to this Matter on Tuesday in the House of Commons. With what object we cannot conceive unless it was to hold up his own party in an unfavourable light. , Sir Henry Campbell Binnerman's reply was crush il3g in its directness and severity, and left no room r for doubt that be and his fellow-ministers hold only one view as to the necessity for absolute irre- '• broachableness in their public characters. ‘laey are all " non-traders," to use a descriptive phrase which is well understood in , Warrington. By the way, the ingenuous Mr. /lay admitted that "the name of the Civil Lard of the Admiralty was included an error" among the A aames of those whom he apparently suspected of qinging to theirdirectorships. " The error serves to remind us," says the Daily News, " that it ' laas a Civil Lord of the Admiralty in the late Oovernment who was found to be a director of a company that supplied goods to his own depart- aaent ; and that that Civil Lord of the Admiralty mould not for the life of him see that such a state , clf things cauld ever conceivably lead to anything tiOaatisfactory." We have met with a similar Obtuseness of moral perception in cases much bearer home and have always regretted that a fligher standard of public service was not volun- Eerily maintained. Thanks to the " non-trading" ' agitation the members of the local Parliament are ompelled to keep themselves above suspicion. conic day, perhaps, as the result of healthy influ- ' noes and the highest examples, the compulsion .11.._a3, he unnecessary. We believe that local, as w_all as imperial.administration is rapidly becoming es from the taint of" self-interest.' Sa may it veer remain !

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

"The proposal to ply M.P.'s £3OO a year is so popular among M.P.'s that Mr. Lever who br night it forward is generally known as " the little Ray of Sunlight.' "—" Tatler. ' * * * Padget° paople purpose planting proper places in Padgate with pretty trees, when they have learned all there is to be learnt from the experience of Stockton Heath.

* * * Mr. A. U. Crosfield, M.P., has been asked to take the captaincy of the Golf Club at Hoylake this year when the amateur championship is played off there. The offer was a tempting one to such a keen sportsman as Mr. Crosfield, but he felt bound to decline owint, to the claims of Parliamentary duties in London.

Saturday was St. Patrick's Day, and though there was a fair showing of Shamrock, it ia as well that we have a fair substitute in clover, for the " dear little, sweet little plant " has been very difficult to gather in Ireland owing to the snow. Nevertheless the sham- rock was conspicuously in evidence at the dinner to Mr. Crosfield, M.P. on Saturday evening—more so in fact than were his Irish constituents.

* * The mountain range which has suddenly risen in Bridge-street and traversed the pavement almost from side to side, it is thought may be due to volcanic action. Probably it will disappear just as quickly. These things often do. At present, however, the passage of the tram-cars along the crest of the moun- tain, and the valiant struggles of cyclists labouring up the gravelly slope, afford much amusement to the. " man in the street."

* * A New York shopper asked for " Lamb's Tales" (from Shakespeare), in a department store. The shop- girl promplty replied : " Fur department, second floor.' In the fur department she, was shown a hand- some set of lynx, and assured that it was made " from the very best part of the link." Asking for a plain brass seal, on which to cut her husband's monogram, she was told they had " brass alligators, brass elephants ; not brass seals."* One of the most pleasing features of the opening of the new Railway Institute at Bank Quay is the admirable way in which the adjoining ground has been laid out. The energetic district manager (Mr. I. T. Williams) hit upon this happy idea of helping forward the Beautiful Warrington movement and his efforts have been worthily seconded by the employees. The place will be quite a bower of beauty in the summer months. . .

*s* A veracious eye-witness relates circumstantially the account of a catastrophe which, he says, befel a large motor car in Sankey-street recently. While proceed- ing cautiously among the many pitfalls which await the unwary driver, the car skidded and sank a yard or more into a puddle. A large number of horses were required to extricate the car, which was successfully accomplished. Unfortunately, during the operations, one of the horses suddenly disappeared in an adjoin- ing hole. We hear that it was a large and valuable " chestnut." A claim for compensation from the Corporation is considere4c,l certain. Our local legislators had quite a field day on Mon- day. For two hours and a half the Town Council debated on the cost of the Bolton School, and hardly had this meeting ended—at 6.3 o—when the proceed- ings of the Education Committee began, and continued until nearly 9 o'clock. There is little prospect of relief from the flood of eloquence, as on Monday next the Council holds another special meeting to consider the Education Committee's neglect to appoint a woman member, and recommendation of the appointment of Mr. A. J. Jolley and Mnt T. May as selected members of the authority, while the Education Committee's annual meeting follows at six o'clock. * * That there is a considerable amount of dissatisfaction with the state of the tree-planting scheme at Stockton Heath no one with a desire to be fair could doubt. We know of people who subscribed for their tree who have felt like Tilling a few up when they have found them interfering with the proper use of the foot- paths. Our old friend Mr. Whitley has been charged with misrepresenting the views of the villagers, but the size of the petition which he is engineering this week proves that he has a substantial backing. We wonder which side will be able to " pack" the parish meeting most effiqiently next Wednesday night. There will not be much else but tree-planting talked.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

* * * Speaking at the complimentary dinner to himself on Saturday evening, the Member for Warrington, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, said "they must not think it was because he was afflicted with any measure of stage fright that he had not fired off his maiden effort in that august assembly yet." He agrees that there is rather to much talking in the House, and his con- stituents can rest assured that when he does make his maiden speech Mr. Crosfield will have something important to say. Talking for talking's sake is very properly tabooed in the very business-like Parliament of to-day. The number of maiden speeches in the early days of the session was a record, and it 'looked rather as if some Members thought their primary duty was to speak at once or for ever hold their peace. * * * Warrington Liberals and Labour men will learn with regret that Mr. Henry Broadhurst M P., has re- signed from the representation of Leicester owing to ill-health. He has spoken in Farr Hall, on several occasions, particularly during the period in which Mr, A. H. Crosfield M.P., was nursing the constituency, and he always had a rousing reception. The "Stone- mason M.P." will be missed from the Lobby of the House of Commons not only because of his sterling character, but as one of its frequenters who was noted for some little eccentricities. His suit of rough brown homespun always marked him apart from his conven- tional colleagues. But he will chiefly be remembered for his thunderous voice which went reverberating down the Lobby, drowning every other sound that swelled in that sonorous atmosphere. * * * It was a pleasure to see Mr. A. H. Crosfield, MP. looking so well at the two functions which lie attended in Warrington last week-end. He is not blessed with robust health, and the strain of Parliamentary attend- ance coupled with residence in London, following upon an arduous election campaign have tried him severely. Both at the congratulatory dinner, and the meeting of the Labour League the Member delivered a lengthy and thoughtful speech which afforded all who heard it great satisfaction. div.p: CARNEGIE LIBRARY AT ASEITON-IN-MAKER- FIELD.

' Lord Gerard on SaturclAy opened the Carnegie Library at Ashton-in-Makerfteld, for which he has given the site. The library has already 3.000 books and room for 2,000 more. There is also in the building a lecture hall to seat 350 persons. LORD NEWTON PORES FUN AT WAR MINISTERS.

---- - Not to be outdone by the Commons, the members qf the House of Lords indulged in a discussion on Monda'y on the militia question.—The discussion was rendered memorable by a witty and caustic speech by Lord Newton.—The Under-Secretary had said that, if the Government were only given time, they would bring everything right. He had heard such statements before. He had seen six Secretaries for War, beginning with Mr. Edward Stanhope, and he had never been able to distinguish between all those eminent persons, although much of their time had been *coupled in pointing out the shortcomings of their prede- cessors. (Laughter.) The same phenomena were always observable in regard to these Ministers. The appointment was hailed with universal approval as that of the one man absolutely fitted to put everything to rights. Then the new Minister made a speech, and the approval became even more vociferous. (Laughter.) At length he produced what was called a scheme, which increased the, admiration for him among people who did not pretend to understand it. (Laughter.) After that these was silence, but in six months time it began to strike people that our military system was in much the same condition as before and after the lapse of a year the paragon had become the most unpopular man in the Government, and the only question was who should fling the biggest brickbat at him. (Laughter).

On Monday evening the subject of the lectur was " A tour in the Highlands of Southern France." In opening, Itlr. div.head: TREE PLANTING AT STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: TREE PLANTING AT STOCKTON HEATH.
Ratepayers' Petition.

Owing to the action of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee at their laNt meeting a petition has been drawn lip and extensively signed, particularly by rate- payers in Whitefleld-road, contradicting the statement that Mr. Whitley's action at the District Council meet- ings, was not representative of the views of the rate- payers of the village. The petition also protests against the trees being planted upon narrow footpaths, and already bears over 180 signatures, several members of the Parish Council being amongst those who have sub- scribed to it. It is also supported by persons who have subscribed to the funds of the Tree-Planting Committee who state that they did not expect that the tree would be placed upon narrow footpaths or would in any way constitute obstructions. The petition takes particular objection to the trees planted in Whitefleld-road, and Fairfield-road, and will ultimately be presented to the District Council. Mr. Whitley desires it to be known that he is not opposed to tree-planting as a general scheme, but that he objects to the trees being planted upon footpaths of a less width then eight feet. He points out that he was first to advocate and practice the beautifying of the village by this means, and adds that he is also an advocate of window boxes &c., and recrea- tion grounds. The ratepayers of the village will have an opportunity of expressing their views, as Mr. J. W. Bouchier, as chairman of the Parish Council, has called a special parish meeting for Wednesday evening next. A report of the discussion at the Runcorn Rural Dis- trict Council meeting will be found on page 7.

div.head: Ellesmere-street Mission Extension.
div.p: Ellesmere-street Mission Extension.

The handsome addition which has recently been made to the Ellesmere-street Mission was formally opened on Thursday. For some time it had been felt that the old corrogated iron building was inadequate to the require- ments of a growing community, and a scheme for its conversion into a more suitoble brick building was approved. Lack of funds made it impossible to carry out the whole of the proposals, and as the most pressing need was for school accommodation this part of the work was first undertaken. At a cost of £6OO a hand- some brick building has been erected at the end of the Mission Chapal, which has indidentally been extended ten feet, in which are three large class-rooms and an assembly room capable of seating over 100 persons. The heating arrangements have been improved by the establishment of a hot-water system, and excellent kitchen accommodation has been pro- vided. Towards the cost of the improvement £250 has been aclually received or promised and it is hoped and confidently expected that no difficulty will be experi- enced in raising the balance of the sum required. When the debt has been wiped off the remaining portion of the improvement will be taken in hand. The opening proceedings aroused considerable interest and were largely attended. A special service was held in the mission at which a powerful sermon was delivered by the Rev. J. T. Gurney, Southport. In the evening a well attended meeting was held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Church, the proceedings being under the Chairmanship of Mr. C. E. Parker. It was not without some little pride that Mr. Isaac, hon. treasurer to the scheme, gave a financial statement, as he said the workers in connection with the Mission were making noble sacrifices on behalf of the cause. He exidained that the complete scheme was not pro- ceeded with at once as they did not believe in incurring liabilities which there was no immediate proipect of their being able to meet. Mr. Isaac entered into the details of the scheme and in conclusion said that "a better bit of old fashioned mission work had never been seen." Mr. C. E. Parker, the' Rev. J. T. Gurney, the Rev. Marshal Johnson, and other gentlemen heartily sup- ported the scheme.

div.head: NEW RAILWAY INSTITUTE.
div.p: NEW RAILWAY INSTITUTE.
Recreation for L. and N.-W. Employees
OPENING CEREMONY.

I A commendable scheme to provide recreative facilities for the Warrington employees of the London and North-Western Railway Company was completed on Thursday evening,when Mr.F. J. Kinsatan,manager of the Northern division of the company, formally opened the handsomely-appointed Railway Institute at Bank Quay. The building was formerly used as District Offices but became vacant by the removal of the staff to the commodious premises at Arpley Station and thanks to the efforts of Mr. I. T. Williams, the district goods manager, it was secured for the purpose of an insti- tute, the object being to provide for the employees ta means of social intercourse, mutual helpfulness,mental and moral improvement, and rational recreation. The innovation is being highly appreciated as the company have 800 employees in Warrington who will be able to avail themselves of the Institute and the sons of employees who reside with their parents will also be eligible for membership. The building and its surroundings have undergone a transformation and will not only be admirably adapted for the pu-rposes named but will be an ornament to the neighbourhood. The first improvement which impresses the visitor is the artistic way in which the land adjoining the institute 7 nag been laid out and planted with trees and shrubs. In summer the garden will be one of the prettiest spots in the town and as the building is also to be covered with creepers the alterations should afford a valuable help to the Beautiful Warrington movement. As showing the interest which the com- pany's workmen have taken in the scheme, it is worthy of note that they have been almost entirely.responsible for the arrangement of the grounds and have under- taken the work in their own time. Mr. Minshull, the permanent way divisional inspector, has been particularly to the fore in this department. Rockeries form a prominent and attractive feature and in time those will be partially hidden beneath a thick growth of ferns. Generous assistance in the provision of shrubs has been received from several leading residents of the district including Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., and the Earl of Crawford. As to the institute itself, the facilities are of the most complete deicription. There is a lecture room capable of seating about 100 people, and here it is propooecl to lecture on technical subjects and also on various local indrstries. Alongside this room an air rifle range has been provided, and mem- bers will he allowed to test their skill with the gun at a charge of ten shots a penny. It is hoped to induce other clubs to take up this latter idea and to form a Rifle League. There is also a fine bagatelle table. Adjoining the lecture room is the recreation room, where chess, draughts, and other games can be induged in under the most pleasant conditions. There is a cosy news room provided with all kinds of publications, and a smoke-room will also be a welcome place of retreat for those wishing to enjoy a whiff of the fragrant weed. One of the main objects of the Institute is to encourage the work of the Ambulance Corps and the Railway Temper- ance Union, and rooms have been allotted for the meetings of these useful organizations. The large billiard room is equipped with a splendid up-to-date table and will doubtless be the scene of many an exciting game. All the rooms are embellished with interesting photographs, and there is a valuable I collection of the products of the chief industrial con- corns in the Warrington District of the Company which embraces practically the whole of the centre and northsof Lancashire. The institute will be under tho management of a thoroughly representative com- mittee, and the chief officers are : President, Mr. I. IT. Williams; vice-presidents, Mr. T. M. Fowke, Mr. IW. M. Turnbull, Mr. W. Williams ; hon. treasurer, Mr. D. Banks ; hon. secretary, Mr. E. Robinson ; hon. assistant secretary, Mr. A. W. Allman. Naturally the opening ceremony was attended by a little speech-making and a large number of the employes assembled in Messrs. Crosfield's assembly room, which was kindly placed at their disposal. Mr. I. T. Williams occupied the chair, and was supported by Messrs. F. T. Kinsman, manager of the Northern Division ; F. Grasemann, Euston ; F. Kinsman, jun., Lancaster ; V. H. Williams, Wolverhampton ; T. M. Fowke, ,livisional engineer, Edgehill ; W. M. Turnbull; W. Williams, chief store keeper, and D. Banks. A letter of apology for non-attendance was received from Mr. Russel Ree, chief goods manager, who had arranged to open the building, but was prevented front being present owing to a business engagement, and who wrote expressing his sympathy with the movement. Others who wrote apologising for non-attendance were were Mr. Dawson. chief assistant engineer ; Mr. Carl Grasemann, Euston ; and Mr. Robert Turnbull, superintendent. Mr. WILLIAMS, who had a very hearty reception, briefly explained the object of the Institute. He ex- pressed his indebtedness and thanks to the many manu- factures who had so readily and generously assisted in the direction of providing specimens illustrative of the industries in the district. In order to assist in the intellectual enjoyment of the men, he announced, many friends had voluntarily promised to give descriptive lectures of the different processes in their manu- factures—lectures which, they would agree, would be of great value. Mr. Williams proceeded to explain that the men were to be encouraged to put forward sug- gestions in regard to the work in the different depart- ments as prizes would be periodically given to authors of the ideas which a committee considered to he the best. A box had been provided at the Institute in which the written sugges- tions could be placed. A special advantage of the new organization was that it was not in any way restricted to a particular class, but was available equally to all departments, all of which were represented on this Com- mittee of Management. It was desired to make the Institute self supporting without any financial help from outside scources. They had received very generous treatment from headquarters, and there was no reason why they should not accomplish what was desired." We start absolutely free from debt " said Mr. Williams in conclusion" I hope we shall keep so." (Applause). Mr. WILLIAMS then, amidst applause, handed a gold key to Mr. Kinsman, to be conveyed by that gentleman to Mr. Ree, together with the sincere thanks of the Warrington employes of the Company for the practical help he had given them and the sympathy he had shown in regard to the institute. A pretty incident, which was warmly applauded, occurred when Miss Robinson appeared on the platform and fpresented Mr. Kinsman with a box of choice orchids from the Mayor's hot houses' for Miss Kinsman. Mr. KINSMAN, having said he yielded to none in the i interest which he took n the Warrington staff, or any other staff, congratulated the Warrington employees upon havinf, so excellent a head as Mr. Williams. (Applause.) The improvement which Mr. Williams had effected in the business of the Company and in the relationship with traders,was well known and recognised at headquarters and he hoped the Warrington staff equally recognized what Mr Williams had done for them. (Applause.) Mr. Kinsman proceeded to con- gratulate Mr. Williams upon having a staff who had succeeded in getting together the necessaries for the establishment of the institute—an effort which reflected the greatest credit upon them. The formation of the institute, said Mr. Kinsman in conclusion, afforded the directors of the Company the greatest possible pleasure and they looked forward with great hope that it would do much to cultivate good feeling amongst the various departments throughout the service. lie hoped the institute would provide a means for social recrea- tion and mutual helpfulness and assured them that any- thing that he or the heads of the Company could do to advance the work they would be only too glad to dos (Applause.) Mr. GRASEMANN also expressed his hearty support of the movement.

On the motion of Mr. W. M. TURNBULL, seconded by Mr. W. WILLIAMS, Mr. Kinsman was heartily thanked for his services, those present cheering and singing " For he's a jolly good fellow." Mr. Williams' popularity amongst the men was amply demonstrated,as a vote of thanks to him for presiding was accorded with equal heartiness. Thanks having been accorded to all who had assisted in the inauguration of the Institute an adjournment was made to the Institute building, which was formally opened by Mr. Kinsman. Mr. Gra.seraan and Mr. Kinsman then opened the billiard table, the first-named winning a short game. The rifle range was similarly opened, and on every hand satisfaction was expressed at the provision which has been made for the social recreation of the men.

div.head: ART MASTER'S POSITION.
div.p: THE ART MASTER'S POSITION.
MR C. B. AYLWARD ASKED TO RESIGN.
Mr. H. Roberts and " So-called Public-Spirited Men!'

There was a lengthy discussion at the monthly meet- ing of the Education Committee on Monday as to the position of Mr. C. B. Aylward,headmaster of the school of art, and the decision of the School Management Committee calling upon him to resign. No reference to the subject was contained in the minutes but the directors of Education in answer to Mr. Lord,said that 1 a letter had been received from Mr. Aylward with refer- ence to the request to him to resign his position, and the matter had been left in the hands of the Chairman of the Committee, the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson. The MAXOFt said he did not understand why such an important matter as that should not come before the Committee in the usual way, instead of being left off the minutes. He had received a letter from someone, stating that Mr. Aylward had been asked to resign with- out any explanation, and he knew nothing about such a thing having been done. He had asked the Chairman privately whether there was anything to come on that night with reference to the art master, and he replied that he did not think so. He (the Mayor) failed to see why the matter had been kept in the dark. If Mr. Aylward was a good servant or a bad one there was no reason why the Committee should not know about it, Considering that there had been so much trouble in the Town Council about things being kept off the minutes he thought this matter was of such importance that the general Committee ought to have known something about it. (Hear, hear.) Councillor LORD: I would like to know by whose authority the minutes referring to it were omitted from the agenda? Mr. PLINSTON said he was pleased that the question had been raised. After the last meeting of the Com- mittee, to his surprise, he found that he had taken part in calling upon Mr. Aylward to resign a position which he had held for 23 years. When they passed the minutes of a Committee they had a right to know what they were doing. He was told that this had been kept quiet out of kindness of heart, but there were some kind things which the people they were done for did not appreciate. It was not an insignificant matter to call upon a head master to resign and he thought it ought not to have been left to the public and the Press to bring this matter fotward. Members of the Com- mittee were in the position of being blamed for having dene something which they had never desired to do. (Hear, hear.) Alderman TINNION thought those who were respon- sible for the omission of the minute were deserving of the gravest censure. The action of the sub-committee was universally condemned in the town, and he thought justly so. The general body of members knew practically nothing of the matter, and the only informa- tion they had to go upon was the circular letter, referred to by the Mayor, which had been sent to them by somebody. He thought both the Education Com- mittee and Town Council had not been fairly treated by the sub-committee in the way they had asked the art master to resign. The matter had got to be faced out, and it might as well be faced out now. It was neither fair to the Committee nor the art master that the matter should have been smuggled through in the way it had. It would not be tolerated and he hoped that when the sub-committee had anything of the sort to do again they would do it a little more straightforwardly than they had on that occasion. Mr. MAY said there was a strong feeling that the suppression of this minute had been a deliberate deception upon those who were not members of the sub-committee. By not giving Opportunity for fair dis- cussion the sub-committee laid the Education Committee open to undergo such humiliation by having their work gone over as it had been by the Town Council that night. Although he thought the proper course had been taken in regard to Mr. Aylward he did not think it was the proper course to suppress this minute. In future he would suggest that any matter it was desired to keep private should be referred to the General Purposes Committee. _

The MAYOR then moved that the minute relating to the Art Master be not confirmed. Mr. PLIN6TON seconded, and Alderman SMETFIIIRST supported. Mr. HENRY ROBERTS said he, for one, was not going to take those insinuations lying down. If the people who had made the statements and insinuations had taken tke trouble to acauaint themselves with the facts they would not have made those statements. The whole of the proceedings relating to the Art Master took place while he (Mr. Roberts) was away, so that personally he had no part in asking the Art Master to resign. At the same time he was not going to question the motives of the sub-committee in wishing, so far as they could —and he believed it was an honest wish—to spare the feelings of Mr. Aylward in giving him notice in the way they did. It was no true friend ' of Mr.Aylward that had raised the question that night. So far back as six or seven year ago it was considered whether some change in the headmastership was not ! desirable in the interest of the school and the scholars. and a warning then administered—a warning which had been repeated on two occasions since. Now the sub. i committee had had to take the bull by the horns and ask i Mr. Aylward to resign a position for which he was never fitted, and was not fitted to-day : He said that with a full SeDSO of the responsibility which its import- I ance implied. When they bad a man so absolutely I incapable of exercising discipline that in giving lessons at school in connection with the teaching of art it was necessary to have a member of the staff present to keep discipline in that small class—well, need he say any- thing more ? The MAYoR : Because be is not tall enough ? (Laughter.) Mr. ROBERTS I know what it is not to be tall enough. Thank God most little men have qualifications , given to them to make up for their want of stature— (laughter)—but he has to be a very big man I am afraid I to meet. (Laughter.) Continuing, he said it was an I exceedingly unfortunate fact that Mr. Aylward lacked I the necessary qualification for a headmastership and no I one sympathised with him more than he (Mr. Roberts) did. When the matter was before the committee he I pleaded very hard that the notice to Mr. Aylward should be withdrawn, because, being over 50 himself he knew how difficult it was for a man who had passed the half century to take up any new departure in life and he succeeded 1 so far that the chairman was empowered to give ' Mr. Aylward the opportunity of resigning himself. He I was sorry the question had arisen that night because the Chairman of the sub-committee had been asked to inter- I view Mr. Aylward, and the reason it was left off the minutes was because the matter was not yet finally settled, and to spare Mr. Aylward'e feelings. He could have thought more e the criticism of the sub-com- mittee if he could respect the motives which prompted ' it. If all the gentlemen who had spoken upon it, inside and outside that room, and written upon itand expressed the various sentiments of their mind, had had one supreme object in view, and that the real solid interest I of the school and the children who attended it he would respect their views, but be knew that was not the I motive. " Any stick is good enough to thrash a dog I with," and that was the spirit which had prompted some of their so-called public-spirited men to drag up any I case, no matter how dirty it was, if they could create for the moment a certain amount of public sentiment to keep their wretched cause alive. That was the top and bottom of the whole business. He did not say everyone who criticised the committee was one of that crew, but the prime movers in it were unfortunately men tarred I with that extremely unenviable reputation ; men who had dragged the good name of the town into the mud I and filth until it had become a by-word throughout the' country; men whose public professions and personal conduct gave the lie one to the other ; and men who personally and collectively were there in many cases for the purpose of serving their individnal interests and in other instances to serve the interest of the collective group. "These are the men, forsooth." he concluded, 1 "who pose as the leaders of public opinion in a town of 70,000 inhabitants. Tam ashamed of them." Councillor MAGINN said he had not intended to speak i on the matter, but after the remarks of Mr. Roberts he could not possibly let it pass. He hoped Mr. Roberts nor anyone else would accuse him of any ulterior motives in the matter. He did not know Mr. Aylward, and did not know what kind of a teacher he was, but all that had been said did not excuse the Committee or the Chairman, or anyone else, from asking them to " sack " a man with 20 years' service without their knowing any- thing about it. If Mr. Aylward deserved the "sack ' as stated then he should have been "sacked" long ago, but apart from that he did not think the Committee should be asked to put a man out of bis position and not know it. Keeping a thing quiet like this caused a feeling of suspicion, and it would be far better for their servants to know that these things should be discussed publicly. Paid out of the public purse, their conduct should be judged publicly, and they should be "sacked" publiclMr. -JOLLEY associated himself with the remark that everything should be straightforward and above board, t and contended that the sub-committee had done right in the matter. The only reason the question was not made public was because i+ was not finally settled, and because they wished to spare Mr. Aylward's feelings, and to avoia injuring his reputation as much as possible. One remarkeible thing had struck him as being peculiar: that those writing to the Press called for publicity anonymously by omitting to sign their names. (Hear, hear,and laughter.) The vilest motives had been ascribed to the Committee whose sole object was to secure efficiency. He thought the names of those forming the sub-committee were guarantee that nothing dishonour- able and mean, as was insinuated, would be done, and

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 24, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 24, 1906.

they were entitled to resent the accusations which some people had levelled at them. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said he was glad Mr. Jolley had pro- tected the honour of the Committee. He moved his amendment, because there was nothing in the letter he had referred to to show that Mr. Aylward was incapable or that he had not done his duty. In tact, the letter was practically a testimony to his having carried out the work properly according to the Government reports . which said the work was satisfactory. If that was so he ought not to be called upon to resign. His own sons went to the School of Art and he thought he had received value for money. Of course there was not the quantity of students now as formerly, as the Technical School took away many and there were other causes. He went through the school about twelve months ago with Mr. Charles and they were thorougly astonished, at the good work whieh was being done there. He did not see why Mr. Aylward should be asked to send in his resignation, but if the Committee would say it was because there was not sufficient scholars or that the , school was in a poor state then matters would be ' different. He hoped Mr. Aylward would not be called upon to resign before they were given reasons for it. Mr. ROBERTS : I have told you why. The MAYOR : We have only your statement. Canon STEVENSON said be was sorry to have heard ! one or two of the expressions which had been used that j night, and he thought it would be better for him to tell the plain tale of what had happened. The report of the year's work at the school was presented to the Committee at the November meeting. He felt it his duty to comment upon it and comments were made by other members present. It was plainly stated that it was thought the town was not getting value for its money. The number in the school had dropped in one year from 250 to 192; the number examined had dropped from 211 to 134; the number of passes from 138 to 62, and the percentage of successes from 65.4 to 4626. All that in one year. Remarks were made upon that and he promised that the School Management Committee would take the condi- tion of the school into their serious consideration. That had been done and they had gone thoroughly into the matter. They felt that the results were had ; that the number of pupils was rapidly decreasing ; and that the school was not filling the place it ought to fill in a town of this size. They couldinot shut their eyes to the fact that the young children who went there were in such a state.of disorder nd unruly discipline that the lessons were a perfect farce. They looked back into the past history of the matter, and found that more than once it had been very plainly suggested to the headmaster that unless an improvement was effected his resignation would be called for. The improvement had not taken place, and after the. careful consideration of the Committee, Mr. Aylward was asked to send in his resignation.To that he replied with the letter the Mayor had referred to. The Committee went through it and, as the members would find, it did not meet either of the two points he had raised, and had no reference to the question of discip- line. While the committee felt that they had only one course open—and that was a very painful one—they thought they might do it in the most considerate manner possible. They recognized the fact that he had been head of the school for 22 years and they therefore wished to bring about his resignation in a way which would be the least painful to him. It was proposed and carried thltt the minute referring to the matter should not be printed on the agenda. Whether they had been right or wrong he did not know, but at all events there had been no wish for deception of any kind, but they had been actuated by an honest desire to spare the feelings of the person referred to. Eventually it was decided that he should interview Mr. Alyward and ascertain what his ideas and feelings were and intimate that if he could see his way to send in his own resig- nation the Committee would try to meet him. The Committee had had an intimation that it was not un- likely that Mr. Alyward, was wishful to resign, and, therefore, he went to interview Mr. Alyward, and was very nicely met. Mr. Alyward N 29 grateful for the consideration shown to him, but he was not able to meet the two points which be (Mr. Stevenson) put to him quite plainly. Mr. Alyward was certainly an artist of a very high order, but he was not a teacher, and that was a lamentable thing ; but it was for them to remem- ber that they were dealing with the school, and the teaching could not be done efficiently if the master had not the power of maintaining discipline. The result of the interview was that Mr. Alyward told him it had been his intention to resign in July, 1907, in any case, and in reply he told him that he (Canon Stevenson) wished he had known sooner as had he done so the Committee would not have taken the step they had because he felt sure they would have allowed the extension of time. lie eventually left on the understanding that Mr. Aylward would think over whether he would like to resikm in 1906 or 1907. The reason the matter was not mentioned on the minutes was therefore that it was not finally settled. He had not left Mr. Aylward very long when he took up a paper and was somewhet taken aback to find that) someone had been cruel enough to put the letter the Mayor referred to in the paper. That was a plain statement of the case, and he was sorry the sob- committee had been misjudged and misconstrued in the way they had. He did not think, however, that their conscience would trouble them. They had tried to act with consideration, and to discharge a painful duty in the most considerate way possible. He thought they would have succeeded if it had not been for the unkind interventionlof those who thought they were the friends of Mr. Aylward. Alderman TINNTON said he was not sorry for anything he had said which had brought about this explanation, because it had cleared the air. He spoke in the interests of Mr. Aylward, the committee, and the public, because as the case had never been stated only on one side, a had impression had got abroad. All that had been said about Mr. Aylward not being a disciplinarian might be right, but he did not think it was fair to blame him altogether. The reduction in the number of children could not be put down altogether to him because he thought the school was not wanted to the same extent as some years ago. It had changed very much, and if the Committee intended to make it as useful an institution as it had been in the past, they would have to make considerable alteration/not only in regard to the master, but in regard to the school generally. The amendment was then put and lost by six votes to 13.

COUOCiIIOr LORD said he had not been informed yet by whose authority the minute was left off the agen,?.a. The CHAIRMAN : By the authority of the Committee. Councillor LORD: But was that resolution recorded for the sanction of this Committee?
Canon STEVENSON : I have always understood that it has been the custom of the sub-committee not to print minutes if there was some good reasons why they should be omitted. _ _
COllnCillOr LORD : That is wrong and only refers to minutes of little importance. The CHAIRMAN: Well, there was no attempt at con- cealment except for the reasons stated. The matter then dropped.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL
By " Nest "

Warrington start winning again t i-day --that is if they are as good as Featherstone Rovers. The opposi- tion will be furnishedlby Widnes who were beaten in a cup-tie at Featherstone by 23 points to 2 last week- end. I think I may fairly assume that Warrington are capable of doing what the junior Yorkshire team did. Widnes are hardly first-class now-a-days whereas Warrington are—sometimes. As a matter of fact Warrington should win every remaining match to the end of the season. Four of the six engagements are at home, and the other two are not very severe ones. Thelist is as follows : Widnes, Roll, lialifax,Hunslet, at home Rochdale Hornets and St, Helens away Three of the matches are during the Easter week-end, which will close the season as far as Warrington's League engagements are concerned. Maximum points from these maining matches would go far towards making Warrington's record more worthy of them,

The exhibition match at Liverpool came off all right, and both Warrington and Runcorn played fine open football. A draw of 15 points each caused the stay-at-homes to smile when they opened their papers, but the result was no pre-arranged affair. There was some keen football, and both Taylor and Moran got damaged, the former with a cut on the lip which has thrown him off the team for the present. Berry, Isherwood and Jordan were seen at their best, while on the Runcorn side Jolley was übiquitous and took a lot of watching. Unfortunately the match was not a success financially, as the notice had been too short to allow of i proper adVertising. The crowd would number about 1.200 and they seemed to think they had had good sport 'for their money.

On Monday, Warrington had to go to Leeds with the usual weak team. Berry was unable to get away, and such useful men as Knight, Dickenson, Taylor, Hockenhall and Boardman on the injured list. Fish turned out again and showed much of his old form, though he will have to get his weight down before he can do those lightning sprints along touch which usually end in a score. Of course, Wa rrington lost at Leeds, but only by a try to nil. The forwards were beaten again, and behind there was nothing brilliant enough to counterbalance. Isherwood for once was off form and dropped a good number of passes. Jordan shaped well again, and a word of praise is due to C. Ashton for the creditable way in which he filled the full-back position. Brooks got his side penalised ifar too often, and in consequence has fallen into dis- favour with the selectors for to-day's match.

The chosen team to play Widnes is : Berry, full backs ; Fish, Isherwood, Jordan and Harris, three- quarters ; Lees and Lambert, half backs; Preston, Belton, Shugars, Heath, Thomas, harmer, Naylor, and Swift, forwards.

I am very pleased to see that young Lambert has been given his chance with the seniors. If" " team form counts for anything he has earned his pro- motion, and I am looking forward to him giving a clever display against the moderate Widnes backs. There is some good"- stuff "in the Salford lad and he ought to train on into the sort of half back Warring- ton have been looking for ever since " Smack "Bate retired from active service. By the way, Lees is persistently spoken of as a "junior " by the notes in the " Chronicle." As a matter of fact the Chadderton man must be about 27 years old, and he had, more- over, a couple of years' experience with the Oldham first team. While not doing anything very brilliant he is playing good football each week.

The cup-ties provided some rare surprises last Saturday—the greatest of which was in my opinion, Keighley's win at Hull. Still Widnes's cropper at Featherstone and the defeat of Oldham and Leeds on their own grounds by Halifax and Broughton were sufficiently sensational. Leigh's humiliation by five tries to nil at Bradford I was not surprised at. Leigh may be league leaders, but they have not gained that position by superiority over the crack clubs in the league. The average -number of visits to Yorkshire would have brought their record down to a level more in keeping with the actual quality of the team. At present they are making the championship secure by cheap points taken from the small fry of the competi- tion. I suppose it pays!

What a great opportunity Warrington missed of repeating their Cup success when they failed to beat Batley in the first round ! The" gallant youths " fairly caught fortune's smiles that day, and in the second round had an easy win over York. Now, Round 3 sees them drawn at home again to the second of last year's finalists. They may very probably beat the Rovers by their paculiar methods,but if the visitors can hold the Batley forwards they should make the issue secure by superiority behind. What a struggle there would have been at Wilderspool if the battle between the cup finalists had had to be fought over again? Ah well !

The draw for the sennd round to be played on the 31st is as follows : Keighly v. Featherstone Rovers. Bradford v. Halifax. Salford v. Broughton Rangers. Batley v. Hull Kingston Rovers. The " A" team gave one of the worst displays this season against Radcliffe Rangers, the winners of the Manchester League. Though they were strongly represented, the combination champions only won by a point,and that was obtained in the last five minutes. There was a fine crowd, attracted by the presence of Fish and Harris in the team, but disappointment was general. The Warrington men all seemed to be at their worst, while the forwards were hopelessly and disgracefully beaten by a lighter pack. Radcliffe tried hard to win and were unlucky to lose by a try to a goal on the days's play. Still on most days I think Warrington " A " would beat them with a dozen points to spare. The "A " team men are resting to-day. It can't do them much harm.

By the way, one of the " A " team forwards I could not see which—was guilty of a piece of brutality born of bad temper which deserves punishment. He deliberately " knocked out" one of the Radcliffe halves with a blow in the face, the poor fellow being completely stunned for a moment. From what I hear the identity of the offending player is known to the Committee. If so, they will ha manifestly neglecting a plain duty if they fail to suspend him for the rest of the season.

A recent school examination elicited the following definitions " Noah's wife," wrote one boy, '' was called Joan of Are." " Water," wrote another, "is composed of two gases, oxygen and cambrigen." " Lava," replied a third youth, "is what the barber puts on your face." " A blizzard," insisted another "is the inside of a fowl." Truly a little know- ledge is a very dangerous thing—even with children. —"Tatler."

div.head: RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.
div.p: RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.
CONTINUED CHURCH OF ENGLAND AGITATION.
Letter from Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P.

----- The Church of England agitation upon the question ofjeligious education continues and during the week a number of meetings have been held. On Monday even- ing a small audience assenbled in the St. Luke's School, Liverpool-road, under the chairmanship of Mr. William Jackson. Councillor FORSHAW proposed :—"That this meet- ing protests against any attempt being made to inter- fere with the religious liberty of parents in the educa- tion of their children." The moment the Government began to take away the religious education of the people that moment they began to knock down the very foundation stcuaeof England's greatness, morality, power and goodness, and he hoped, therefore, that they would with all their mind and strength oppose any such thing. (Applause.) The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON seconded, and alluded to what he described as "passive resisters "advertising their consciences. It was not an expensive aFlvertise• merit and could be obtained very often for a few shillings. (Laughter.) With regard to Free ChFch- men,. look at their ideas of freedom. They proposed to deprive Churchmen of what their forefathers had given for the instruction and education of their children. The schools in which they were then assembled were built by snob Churchmen as the late Lord Winmarleigh, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. Beamont and others, and the schools in Museum-street were built in the same way. To whom were they given?—to the Churchpeople of the district for educational purposes, and the trust deed said that those who built them did so that they might be used for the education of the people of the district in religious and useful knowledge and for no other purpose but Free Churchmen said "No. Church- men shall not use them for that purpose. They shall give not the church teaching for which the schools were actually provided, but some sort of teaching we approve," and in future the rates to which Churchmen contributed quite as much as Free Churchmen did were not to be used for giving any teaching except that which Free Churchmen approved. Some -went further and said it was better to get rid of religion altogether. That was the sort of domineering tone they adopted and also the domineering action they would take unless a stop was put to it. Their object was to deprive Churchmen of the benefits which had been secured to them by their friends and benefactors in the past. So they saw.how much freedom there was amongst Free Churchmen. (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. H. J. WESTBROOK moved :—" We demand that the rights of all denominations have full and equal recognition with respect to religious instruction in our elementary schools.' Mr. H. T. DEAN seconded and the motion was carried The Chairman was thanked for his services on the motion of the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, seconded by Councillor FonsriA.w. Letter from Mr. A. H. Crosfleld.

Mr. Peter Edgar has received the following letter from Mr. A. EL Crosfield, M.P. : " Dar Sir, I have your favour of Maruh 6th in regard to the Education 'Question, and the resolution passed at St. Peter's Church congregational tea party. We are all agreed that the measure passed by'the late Government was no settlement of the Education difficulty at all, and so the present Government has to tackle the question of education further, and it is the most difficult problem it has to solve. I will give the matter, I can assure you, close and careful attention, and may have the privilege of writing you on the matter g little later on St. Ann's Church.

A meeting of the parents attending St. Ann's School was held in the Dannett-street schoolroom on Tuesday evenirfg,,the Rev. J. Davies presiding. Resolutions were adopted, copies of which will be 'sent to Mr. A. IL Crosfield, M.P., and the Minister of Education,. protesting against the elimination of definite religious instruction in the schools, and against any action which would alienate the property held in trust for giving religious education. Meeting at Stockton Heath. A well-attended meeting was held in the Church Room, Stockton Heath, on Tuesday evening, Mr. William Richardson in the chair. The CHAIRMAN said the time. had arrived when Churchpeople should be heard in no unmistakable manner upon this important and vital question of religious teaching in our Church schools. They were not met to attempt to thrust their religious beliefs down the throats of those who differed from them. They were not met to claim a monopoly of conscience; not for political purposes, but to pronouncetheir determina- tion to resist at all cost, any attempt to deprive them of their undoubted rights to teach the children of Churchmen and women their religion, by their own teachers, in their own schools ; schools built and main- tained by Churchpeople, mindful of their duty to their country and their religion. (Applause.) The Rev. J. COLLINS read the petition which those present were requested to sign. The petition stated that Churchmen would oppose any legislation—(l) Which wonld either establish, at the expense of the whole community, a form of undenominational religion for all schools throughout the country, or .would give to any denomination religious privileges not accorded to others; (2) which would place the Bible in the hands of teachers whose belief in the Christian Faith and whose qualifications and ability to teach religion may not in any way be tested ; (3) which would aleniate propeillty held in trust for giving religious education ; (44 which would interfere with the power to give in school hours by the clergy and school staff (subject to a Conscience Clause) religious teaching in accordance with the trust debd. Applause.) Mr. POTTS moved 'That this meeting adopts the petition which has been read to-night and earnestly recommends it for signature." (Applause.) Mr. H. J. WESTBROOK seconded. They were told that it was quite wrong for Dissenters to pay for the teaching of a religion which they did not beliewe. If Dissenters were the only ratepayers that would be quite right, perfectly right ; but were they the only rate- payers? Did they pay even the amount of rates whioh ChUrchmen paid? The children were not the children of the State but of the parents, and the parents were responsible for the spiritual life of the children, and they had a right to say that the money contributed to the rates should be allocated to the teaching of the Gospel in which they believed. (Applause.) Mr. F. Pearson, Mr. J. H. Clarke and Mr. S. W. Dallow also spoke in support of the resolutiOn. The Rev. H. A. LESTER said they wanted fair treat- ment and no favour. Let the Roman Catholics, the Jew and the Wesleyan have their rights, but what had the Church done that it should not be treated fairly and ; squarely? They were, however, determined that the ; Church should be treated fairly arid squarely. (Applause.) They must see that the empire did not suffer and decline • because of the action of certain people who were I jealous of the Church of England. It was the religion of England which had made it what it was to-day, and I• if they wished to maintain their faith in the God of nations, and their character for national righteousness they must see that the young had the seeds of righteons- ness implanted in their hearts. (Applause.) i The resolution was carried unanimously. 1 Mr. DUNN proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman I and gave directions as to the signing of the petitions. ; Mr. H. GREENALL seconded and the motion was carried.

div.head: "AGONY TO WEAR CLOTHES !"
div.p: "AGONY TO WEAR CLOTHES !"
Terrible Attack of Eczema Taken Just in Time with Zam-Buk.

Mr. Lewis Robinson, who lives at 480, Harewood Street, Leeds Road, Bradford, said to a local pressman: "My weeping eczema started with an almost unendur- able itch, but'. for a time there was no blemish on my skin. Then I began to be covered with blotches, which rapidly spread to every part of my body except my face and neck. You could scarcely have got a pin head in between the blotches. The irritation was so great that for a fortnight I did not average more than three hours' sleep a night. It seemed impossible to alleviate my sufferings, or to chock the disease, no matter what I tried.

_ "After a while it got worse, and the blotches on my hands turned to unpleasant black scabs. I pulled them off and this made things worse still. I play the piano professionally, but while the disease lasted I daren't expose my hands, they were in such a terrible state. The blotches on my body had by this time also become scabs, and as I had made sore places by scratching, it was agony to wear my clothes. " The doctor told me it was a bad form of eczema, but his medicine and ointments had not the slightest effect. Nor had the numerous blood mixtures, herb preparations, and ordinary ointments that I tried. Five weeks were spent in trying these useless treatments. The itching had now become terrible, and I was afraie to go out. "Then I read of Zara-Buk, and immediaaely bought a large box. At night I rubbed the balm all over my body, and the itching was so eased that I slept soundly. I awoke to find the itching quite gone, and when I touched my arms and legs the scabs burst, discharging a watery matter. The diseased tissue began to peel off right away, and as [continued the applications of Zam- Buk a beautiful, new, soft skin was revealed. Alto. gether I used ten boxes of Zam-Buk, and my skin is now quite free from blemish. My brother contracted the disease, though in a milder form, through sleeping with me. div.head: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
THE STAFFING OF THE SCHOOLS.
Physical Instruction.

The concluding meeting for the year of the Warring- ton Education Committee was held at the Town Hall on Monday. Alderman Bennett presided and there were also present the Mayor, Alderman Smethurst and Tinnion, Councillors Sankey, Ellison, Brough,Wilkinson Burton, Maginn, Fulton Smith, Barton and James Evans, the Revs. Canon Morley Stevenson, N. Wilson, and John Tongs, Messrs. H. Roberts, C. E. Parker, H. Kingdon, R. T. Fairclough, J. D. Buckton, W. Bibby, T. May, GI. Walker, E. Plinston, J. Upson and J. Moore Murray (director of education). V REPRESENTATIVES ON THE COMMITTEE.

It was reported that the Council had decided to refer back the recommendation of the Education Committee for the appointment of Air. Alfred A. Jolley, and Mr. Thomas May as selected members of the committee in view of the opinion of the Council that one of the selected members should be a woman.
Councillor ELLISON moved that Mr. Jolley and Mr. May be again nominated. Mr. PLINSTON seconded, and the proposal was unani- mously carried. THE STAFFING OF THE SCHOOLS.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of the School Management Committee, Canon Morley Stevenson said a small change had been made in the rules regulating the staffing of the schools, it having been decided that, in those schools having an average attendance of 300 children and over,the head teacher should not be counted on the staff, and in those of less than 300 children the head teacher be counted as equivalent to 30 children in average attendance, instead ot 60 as prescribed in the Code. The staffing of the schools was not altogether perfect, and he hoped there would be no objection to that small concession. The MAYOR : What is the advantage of this? Canon STEVENSON: We get a better staff. Alderman SucTfluitsT : At an increased cost. Canon STEVENSON said that in a few cases, "a very few he was afraid, an additional member of the staff would be required to be added. Continuing he said that with reference to the decision of the committee with respect to teachers under 36 years of age qualifying themselves to give physical instruction he had received a letter from the Warrington Certificated Class Teachers' Association protesting against the proposal. The letter read :—" The members of the Warrington Certificated Class Teacher's Association (which/associa- tion includes practically all the certificated class teachers engaged under the Local Education Authority) view with deepest concern the proposed resolution requiring that class teachers under 35 years of age shall obtain a drill certificate before a specified date. Respectfully would they submit that the teachers certificate is a final diploma empowering its holder to teach all obligatory subjects of the Education code and to superintend pupil teachers. They would also point out that upon the introduction of a new subject into the edueation code, existing teachers have always been recognized by the Board of Education as qualified to teach such subjects without special examination. Recognizing that physical instruction is but one of the many subjects in the syllabus for elementary schools, the certificated class teachers, engaged under the War- rington Education Authority respectfully ask that the proposed resolution may be withdrawn."He was rather surprised that the teachers had taken that line. The corn- committee were willing to recognize any reasonable certificate—and a very large number of their teachers held certificates—qualifying them to give physical instruction. He did not think there would be any difficulty in regard to the teachers qualifying them- selves. He did not see that any hardship was being inflicted upon the teachers as a reasonable date had been fixed for them to obtain the certificates. Councillor FULTON SMITH seconded. The MAYOR referred to the proposed alteration of the staffing of the schools. That was one of the most serious matters in regard to expenditure which had been before the Committee for some time. It would prac- tically involve an expenditure of £2,400 per annum on increased staffs, a seal equal to 23,d. in the R. They would not get the Council to pass the item until they thoroughly understood it. He moved that that minute be not confirmed. Alderman SMETHURST seconded on the ground of expense. If it was going to give the teachers more time for book-keeping by employing another teacher he strongly objected to it. Mr. J. D. BUCRTON supported the minute. He ques- tioned the Mayor's figures and pointed out that under present arrangements in small schools teachers had to take two classes. In such cases, where the headmaster was responsible for one or two classes, it was impossible for him to properly supervise the work of the school and do his own work. _
Mr. H. ROBERTS : The Mayor has found another mare's nest. (Laughter.) The MAYOR : Not so much of a mare's nest,

Mr. ROBERTS Wait-Qlll I have finished. It is quite evident that your strong point is not finance or you would not make such a statement as the one which you have made. I deprecate very strongly these repeated attempts to mislead the public of Warrington as to the real position with regard to the cost of education. Con- tinuing he said they had been too long without having to bear that expense which, a due regard to the educational interests of the town would have imposed upon them. Now they had no opportunity of escaping they were kicking against their duty. It would be one of the most hideous blunders which could be per- petrated if they starved their schools at the present time. They were not considering a maximum in regard to the staffing of the schools but were dealing with something less than a minimum of what the Board of Education considered necessary. He protested with all the force of his nature against such a dereliction of 'duty and against false issues being raised. Proceeding Mr. Roberts th-gued that the proposal was absolutely necessary in the interests of the efficiency of the schools. in- stead of costing 2',d. in the B the alteration, at the end
of the two years, would mean an increased cost of 4400.
Mr. MAY asked if the work of the head teachers had been increased so as to necessitate the proposal to decrease their works.

The Rev. N. WILSON said the work had not increased but their head teachers were over-worked. It was absolutely necessary, he contended for the welfare of the schools, that the head teachers should be free from the responsibility for any particular class. He pointed out that in certain schools the number of teachers had diminished whilst the number of the classes remained unaltered.

Mr. A. Js JOLLEY said the decision of the committee had not been hastily arrived at but was the result of most prolonged and careful investigation. They did not desire to unwarrantably decrease anyone's work, their sole object being the securing of greater efficiency in the schools,and, as an education authority that ought to be their primary object. The proposal far from being al revolution try one was very modist and would involve only a very slight additional expense. The committee was very much behind other authorities in respect to its staffs and the school inspectors had fre- quently urged the carrying out of drastic reforms. Mr. Jolley in conclusion urged that the head teachers ought if possible, to be given greater leisure in which to superintend the work of the school. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH supported the minute. His experience of school management was that head teachers should be a free hand. _ _

Mr. J. UPSON said the school staffs in Warrington were at present the irreducable minimum. The pro- posal would only affect seven schools and would not mean an outlay even so much as stated by Mr. Roberts. In a school they were teachers of varying capacity and the head teacher had to be constantly looking after and advising the weak members. To him the proposed reform was the least they could do. Councillor MAGINN desired to know the increase in the number of children during the last four years and also the increase in the number of teachers during the same period. The education rate had advanced 3d. in the £ and apparently it would advance another 3d. next year. and he would like to know what benefit the children had obtained from the increased expenditure. He opposed the proposal on the ground of expense. Canon STEvaxsoN said there were at present in War- rington five small schools which were indisputably under-manned and would have an extra teacher given to them by the proposal. The measure of assistance I asked was so small that he was almost ashamed to mention it. Upon a vote being taken, the Mayor, Aldermen Smethurst and Tinnion,Councillors Sankev,Lord,Maginn, and Burton voted for the motion, Messrs. Upson, Plinston, Walker, Parker, Roberts, Jolley, Buckton, Fairclough, Kingdon, and the Revs. N. Wilson, Canon Stevenson and J. Yonge voting against. The minute was then approved. VOTES OP THANKS. At the close of the meeting Alderman Bennett was heartily thanked for his services as chairman during the year and a similar vote was accorded to Alderman Pierpoint for his services as vice-chairman.
