div.head: STATE OF SANKEY-STREET.
div.p: THE STATE OF SANKEY-STREET.

My Dear Children, The prizes in connection with the two monthly competitions have all been awarded, and I will now give you the names of the lucky winners, and the prizes I awarded. I gave four prizes in connection with the Doll Dreksing Competition as number three and four were so close. The first prize of a beautiful Photo Album was sent to Lillian Deakin, this doll was beautiffilly dressed and the work was very fine. Mary Richardson received the second prize which was a work cabinet, and I consider that this was well deserved for the excellent needlework. Margaret Press was sent the third prize of a handkerchief and glove case, and May Austin received the fourth prize of a silver mounted purse. I had great difficulty in selecting the three best handwriting competitors among the boys, and finally decided to award the first prize to Ernest Harrold; as his specimen was very beauti- fully written and so neat, he has received a writ- ing desk, which I think he will find very useful. The second prize of a pretty writing case was awarded to Henry Shercliffe, and the third prize, a box of chocolates, has been sent to George Richmond. I hope you all like these prizes and that You will write and tell me what you think of them, All those who competed and have not Won prizes must not lose heart but try again, as I shalroffer many more prizes during the next few months, and you all stand equal chances. I shall award a prize to the one who sends me the first correct solutions to the puzzles printed below. These were sent me by Freda Well- bourne, and I thank her for the contribution. xt week I shall give full details of our Flower "Ow Competition, so be sure and look for my etter so that you all may be able to compete. With all good wishes from
UNCLE NED.

Dear Uncle Ned, I am writing to you to tell you my sister's age and name. She is called Lizzie, and her age is xi years. I was overjoyed when I saw my story in print, and I hope I have secured a prize; if so, let me know next week. I have tried hard to secure one.

On March 3rd I am going to try for a labour Certificate, which will enable me to leave school though I am only iz years of age; but, if I pass, I shall continue my school career again. I hope to try again for one of your beautiful prizes before long. I have sent my hand-writing for competition. From your loving Nephew,_ ERNEST HARROLD.

MR. NOBODY. I know a funny little man, As quiet as a mouse, Who does the mischief that is done In everybody's house. There's no one ever sees his face, And yet we all agree, That every plate we break was cracked By Mr. Nobody.

'Tis he who always tears our books, And leaves the door ajar; He pulls the buttons off our shirts, And scatters pins afar. That squeakirig, door will always squeak; So, pri'thee, don't you see, We leave the oiling to be done BY Mr. Nobody. From ERNEST HARROW.

THE THREE FISHES. CHAPTER lI.—THE RESULT OF JOHN'S WISHES. Now we will return, and see how John got on. A few minutes after Jack had taken his hasty departure, John woke up to find a dozen young bloaters laughing at him, He instantly went to bully them, but they all went for him, and he; 'like the coward he was, swam away as fast as he could. Bye and bye he began to feel hungry, so he looked for something to eat. 'After searching for a long while he discovered a worm, so he ate it and was going away, when a hook stuck in. his mouth and pulled him on the land, where a monster, called a man, put him in a bottle cif water. There he tried vainly to get out till he was saved, as will be told in chapter three. So John's wishes came to pass in the befie-men- toned manner.

CHAPTER lII.—SAVED. Meanwhile, Bill, had heard of his brothers' mis- fortunes, and began using his wishes. With the first two he was going to save Jack and John, and leave the third for another time. He was trying to plan which way to start, when he was caught in a net, and taken ashore and put on the ' floor, beside the bottle with his brother in. While struggling there, he knocked over the bottle with his brother in, and the water in it washed both him and has brother into the sea. When Bill recovered he could not see his brother anywhere, but after a little while he found a fish hook with
twi

some line attached to it. This he tied to a rock near the octopus's home. When the octupus saw the hook, which was bated with fish poison, he gobbled it up, and, smacking his great jaws, was going away, when something stuck in his stomach, so he tried to throw it up, but it only pained him more. Then something else pained him; this time it was all over With him. He be- came worse, and the enormous fish slashed the water with its numerous arms, while, mad with pain, it became weaker and weaker. Then the Great Doctor came, the doctor who cures all pain and diseases for man, beast, fowl and. fish alike.

The great fish was dead. Then Bill let Jack loose from his prison, and they went home to- gether, where they met John. Never again did they tease Bill, for he had proved himself superior to them, for Bill was the saviour of Jack and John. (To be continued.)

My Dear Uncle Ned. I am sending you a true story which is en- titled:—
A FATAL LEAP.

Using the slight cover afforded by Mimosa thorn bush, a lion tvaited patiently whilst three antelopes were grazing and getting nearer and nearing, little suspecting the presence of their terrible enemy in ambush only a few yards from them. Crouching still lower in Order to avoid being seen, the lion waited until one of the luck- less beasts approached within half-a-dozen strides of him, and then, seizing the opportunity bounded on his victim with a magnificent roar. Dashing away for dear life, the antelope rushed towards the edge of the precipece, as if it was mad with rage. Gaining on it at every stride—for it is well known that at a few yards distance a lion's speed is terrific—the savage beast overtook it at the edge of the precipice. Heedless of this danger the antelope strained every nerve` to reach the edge; the lion clinging firmly to his victim per- ceives his danger too late, tumbled off with the antelope, and reached the bottom with a terrible ..hud. The antelope escaped one danger only to meet its doom with another; while the lion de- prived of his prey died beside his intefided.victim. I remain, Your ever loving nephew, ARTHUR FEAR N.

Warrington Lose at Leeds

The postponed match between Warrington and Leeds was playea at Headingley on Monday before only 1?000 speotatsirs. Neither side was at full strength, Warring- ton being without Hockenhall, Berry Boardman, Dickenson and faylor. The return of Pfsh and Harris to the three-quarter line was a gratifying feature. Mr. J. Priestley, Salford, was the referee and the teams lined out as follows

_ Leeds— Lavelle, back; Naylor,Thomas, T. Llewellyn, and W. Llewellyn, three-quarter backs; Ward and Bray- shaw, half-backs; Jenkins, Hewlett (capt.), Davison, Wainwright, Moon, Burnley, Wormald, and Birch, forwards.
Warrington—Ashton, back ; Fish, Isherwood, Jordan, and Harris, three-quarter backs ; Brooks and Lees, half backs; Preston, Harmer, Heath, Thomas, Swift, Naylor, Morrison, and Shugars, forwards. . . _

Having lest the -toss War-rington had to face the breeze which blew diagonally across• the field, in the I first half. The game opened with a number of kicking exchanges, which ended to the Warringtonians' advan- tage. Ward, however, sent them back by finding touch with a tall and judicious punt. The Warrington backs, defended gamely but could not prevent the scoring of a fine try. Brayshaw got the ball from a scrummage inside his own half and whipped it out to T. Llewellyn. That player dashed away and handed off several oppon- ents, then giving the ball to Ward. After gaining further ground Ward transferred to Brayshaw, and the last-named forced his way over. The goal kick was a failure. The only other incidents of note in this half' were the clever wing play of Fish, who, after sprinting i round his own backs, put n a kick which very emphati- cally turned the Leeds attack into defence ; a good dribble bv Wormald and Hewlett ; and good full back play by Lavelle. The interval arrived with Leeds leading by a try. Hewlett restarted the game, Isherwood's reply being %follored by kicking exchanges. Leeds had the first attack, but it was checked by a brilliant sprint on the part of Fish, who crowned the effort by getting in a kick which placed Leeds in their own "25." The home forwards, however, worked their way back again to the I Warrington quarters,where some tight scrummages were I fought. T. Llewellyn was given the ball by Brayshaw,' but when appearing dangerous the Leeds centre was finely "grassed" by Jordan. Ashton raised the Beige by I kicking well. Then the Leeds backs got going, but Naylor spoiled the movement by kicking too far. In ' the last few minutes Jenkins put in a strong run, but slipped when appearing dangerous. The end came ith Leeds the winners by a try (3 points) to nil. WEDNESDAY'S MATCHES. div.head: Petition By Shop-Keepers.
div.p: Petition By Shop-Keepers.

Sankey-street has so long been in a shockingly bad condition as regards paving that the shop-keepers of the neighbourhood have at last combined their com- plaints in a petition to the Chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. The petition, which has been signed by every shop-keeper (or his representative) in Sankey-street, reads as follows :

March 15. "ro the Chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee Dear Sir, "We, the undersigned, urgently draw your attention to the deplorable condition of Sankey-street. During the wet weather there is an almost continual shower of , mud splashed from the holes in the surface of the road and thrown on to the shop-fronts by passing vehicles, and one can hardly walk along Sankey-street without getting one's clothes splashed in the same way. We beg you to use your influence to have the whole street repaired as soon as possible."

div.head: SHOCK FOR WIDNES.
div.p: A SHOCK FOR WIDNES.

The visit of the Widnes team to Featherstone attracted the biggest crowd of the season, and as the local team made further progress in the Cup competi- tion by a really substantial score against the League team, the Rovers may congratulate themselves on having provided the sensation of the second round. Robshaw commenced the game with the climatic con- ditions in opposition, but the Widnes defence was soon tested, and after many good attempts Kellett showed fine judgment, and passing out to Hoyle that player scored, Robsbaw, failing at goal. Widnes afterwards was seen to advantage, and Tilley I placed a penalty goal, but the Rovers again asserted themselves, and the Widnes defence was thoroughly tested. Nothing, however, was scored, and the interval ead for the Rovers was only one point. The second half saw the home team in brilliant form, and Evans opened the scoring after Kellett and Pawson bad indulged in fine combination. Robson easily placed the goal, and encouraged by the further success the Rovers forwards kept the Widnes backs fully occupied, play being all in the visitors quarters. Two tries were scored in quick succession, and Robshaw improving one the last quarter of an hour found the home :team in possession of a comfortable lead of eleven points. The rout of the League team was continued, for before time was called Evans again scored two tries, and Robehaw converting both, the final reading was :—Featherstone. 4 goals, 5 tries (23 points) ; Widnes, 1 goal (2 points), , SECOND ROUND.—REPLAYED TIE.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES.

Warrington and Runcorn at Liverpool. With the idea of fostering the Northern Union game in Liverpool and assisting in the formation of a Liver- pool City Club,Warrington and Runcorn played a friendly match on the Edge-lane ground on Saturday. Owing to the hasty arrangements the match had not been properly advertised and the crowd did not number much more than 1,000. Both teams were strongly represented and gave' a very attractive exhibition. The weather was beautifully fine but a strong wind had considerable influence on the play. The teams were as follow : Runcorn : Woods, back ; Allen Moran, Butterworth, and Deakin, threequarters ; Jolley and ‘Vatton. half- backs ; Walker, Richardson, Williams, Patdbury, Dixon, Dobson, Leyland and Smith, forwards. Warrington : Berry, back; Jordan, Isherwood,Taylor and Kenyon, threequarters; Lees and Brooks, half-backs; Heath, Thomas, Morrison, Swift, Harmer, Shugars, Belton and Preston, forwards. . _

Runcorn had to face ,the strong breeze during the first half, and Richardson's initial kick was ably met by Berry, this reply being succeeded by the Warrington forwards making considerable headway and endangering the Runcorn goal. The game was brilliantly contested, ,1 and[after Taylor bad placed Warrington in an advan- tageous position, Moran retaliated and made an opening 1 for Butterworth,who was grassed by Taylor on the verge of scoring. Kenyon intercepted a pass from Watton, and Warrington once more taxed the Runcorn defence and eventually Kenyon got in at the corner, Preston placing a goal from a difficult angle. This success was the means of Runcorn pressing. At this stage Moran (Runcorn) and Taylor (Warrington) collided and both players had ultimately to retire. Isherwood and Jordan were pia lug a magnificent game and the latter man was all but over, Woods being the sole stumbling block. Belton started a dribbling bout and the game was transferred to the Runcorn twenty-five. From a pass by Lees to Isherwood the ball travelled along the line, eventually reaching Jordan, who had no difficulty in ,adding another try for Warrington. Preston took the placd kick, but the ball however,went wide. Moran returned and immediately a free kick was awarded Runcorn, but it was not of much advantage. div.head: Mr. Crosfield M.P. and the Milner Resolution.
div.p: Mr. Crosfield M.P. and the Milner Resolution.

Sir,—How far is a new member entitled to exercise his own judgment in either withholding support from, or voting against a Government he has been returned to support? It is a question which of course has faced many a new corner to the House, and I fancy must have occurred to not a few of us in the debate that took place last night. Had the Government's amendment to Mr. Byle's resolution been such as to whitewash Lord Milner, or the policy under his regime in South Africa, which is generally known as " Milnerism," I am pretty certain a good many who voted with the Government would have been unable to do so—and your humble servant would have been one of them. The resolution however, only referred to one action of Lord Miler's, and although it was not only a mistake (as he has admitted, and for which he has expressed regret), but a mistake of a very grave character and leading to shocking consequences— still after Mr. Churchill's speech I think a vote in loyal support of a Government one so thoroughly admires was not inconsistent with opinions I have freely enough expressed in Warrington, and which are held by many of our friends there, who have condemned as emphati- cally as myself the policy leading up to the late terrible war in South Africa, and the conduct of affairs there on critical occasions during and since that war by Lord Milner. The amendment no doubt was a compromise, and both the Leader of the Opposition and Mr. Chamberlain were bitterly sarcastic at the expense of the Government for, as they in effect put it," damning Lord 111ilner with faint praise." To say the least we have treated him with extreme leniency.— Yours etc., A. H. CROSFIELD.

div.head: What is Justice.
div.p: What is Justice.

------ Sir,—One is almost forced now-a-days to ask what is it that constitutes the great drawback of our country's magisterial benches. I suppose we must to a certain extent give our magistrates the benefit of the doubt ; that is, if there is a doubt. Some of our magistrates we are proud of. After all, there are elements, which beyond doubt, are very prominent in too many of them namely, ignorance and discourtesy. The reason for this no doubt, is to be found in the fact that the qualifica- tions for the office are too low. Stress is laid on pocket and not on ability, on party connection and not on wisdom. What is the result? The public are loosing faith in our Courts of Law. Prisoners prefer being tried before a Jury rather than to trust the ignorance and discourtesy of a man who happens to be a magistrate's chairman once or twice a year. At the Warrington, Police Court on Thursday morning, I could not help asking myself: What is justice? A number of passive resisters were summoned to appear in court " to show cause" why they refused to pay certain amounts of money. They showed courtesy to the magistrates by appearing in court. But how were they treated. Saying the least, they were men, yes, and respectable men. Yet, they were snubbed by being refused a hearing ; does that mean justie ? Their questions were ignored; does that meafi justice? They were bullied away without having a chance to defend themselves; does that mean justice ? If it does, then I will ask : What is the difference between justice and tyranny? I have been wondering whether the law allows such a thing; or is it an abuse of authority ? If the law allows it, I say, such a law is a disgrace to civiliza- tion. If the law does not allow it, then I ask the press in the interest of the public to denounce and condemn such cqnduct. W. J. ROBERTS.
Parker-street.

The Roman Church's Claim to Privilege. Sir,—The claim to a privileged position as regards Education made on behalf of the Roman Churth is a sign of the times. That a claim of this kind should be made by Roman Catholics over the English Catholics should at any rate open men's eyes to the aims at ascen- dancy which Rome keeps steadily in view. That men, Englishmen and Irishmen born, should choose to be designated Roman Catholics is itself an anomaly—an anomaly that would at once be recognized if they chose to style themselves French Catholics or German Catholics ; but it is a much more serious thing when those assuming this mark of foreign allegience openly lay claim to favours under the constitution which are to be withheld from the ancient Church of the land. The foreign designa- tion is a distinct discount on nationality ; and indeed every true Romanist has his nationality qualified by an a priori allegiance to a foreign authority that claims to wield temporal as well as spiritual power ; and it is time that attention should be called to this when a claim is set up to special state privileges for a body that is under so serious a disqualification. I am aware that as a usual thing the foreign epithet is kept out of sight as much as possible by our Roman Catholic friends. The term Roman is apt to be dropped for all ordinary purposes and the innocent term Catholic does duty alone. But it cannot be got rid of, for the Roman Church has sought to give it an authority equivalent to the affirmations of the ancient creeds in the new Articles that she added near four hundred years ago to the Creed of Nicea ; and, however it may be kept out of of sight for a while, every pervert when he gets to a certain point finds that submission to this foreign authority is the one thing essential to his or her admission to communion. It is the one article of faith, adhesion to which is indispensible. Surely a strange thing that this article of faith should not be found in any of the ancient creeds. Leaving however the theological aspect of the ques- tion may I say that the foreign character of the Roman authority is a thing that ought to concern our Irish Nationalist friends quite as much as Anglican Church- men. This foreign authority is just as likely to be loyal the nationalist aspirations of the Irish as to the nationalist aspirations of any other country ; and that is just as long as the Roman Church finds it convenient. Nationalities have been played with in the past and made use of by the Roman Church and then thrown over when the purpose of the hour has been served. Irish history is itself not without an illustra- tion of this. I refer to the statute of Kilkenny passed in 1367, which the Irish historian D'arcy M'Gee calls the Penal Code of race, a statute which enforced the English language and English habits and English laws upon the native Irish, boy- cotting their trade and the race generally in the matter of ecclesiastical preferments. Now it is well known that the Roman hierarchy in Ireland were parties to this statute. The names of three archbishops and five bishops appear as having given their assent and support to the statutes. In those days it suited the Roman Church to support the English sovereign and they did it ; ust as three centuries before it suited the Roman authority to aid the Norman invader to crush out the old English nationality in this country. And in both penal laws followed in the wake of invasion with the Church's approval.—l am, Re., E. C. E. CARLETON. 23rd March, 190 C.

div.head: Religious Teaching in "Their Schools."
div.p: Religious Teaching in "Their Schools."

Sir,—Newspaper controversy, even of a friendly char- acter absorbs so much time, that my rule has been never to notice anonymous letters. This rule I have never broken. I only notice now "Fair Play's" letter— to whom my thanks are due for his kind personal refer- ences, and whose anonymity is however but a thinly- veiled disguise—because it contains statements he and others implicitly believe, because they have been so taught. Incidentally my reply may refute one or two of the statements contained in the sermon recently preached by the Rev. Canon Stevenson. Again I utterly deny the right of Churchmen and Roman Catholics to speak of the schools which they control as " their schools." First, they cannot close them at all. If they were " their's " they could. Secondly, I have before me some Government returns. I find ten schools in Warrington received .£4,839 towards their erection ; eight of these schools are Anglican. They cost £10,767; of this £7,142 were given in subscrip- tions, &c., while the remainder £3,625 came from grants. One Roman Catholic school received £6Bl towards its erection while its promoters subscribed £1,543. Again the annual grants for educational purposes alone, in 1899 came to £17,711. How does this square with the claim the monopolists make to "their schools" ' • built by their own " blood and treasure?" For the whole country the figures stand thus (Vide Government return bd 1,336 for 11,02 p. iv.) : (1) 6,765 Denominational and Private schools received Government grants. (2) 5,465 of these were Anglican schools. (3) 87 were Roman Catholic schools. (4) 300 other schools, namely 190 unsectarian schools, and 110 Wesleyan schools received building

grants. (5) Total building grants to Anglican schools £1,5T5,205; to Roman Catholic. schools, £50,579 ; to British and other schools, £201,00 ; total £1,766,854. These returns show (a) That education is public. (b) That the erection of sectarian schools is in part a public charge. (c) That the claim of the Sectarians to their schools" is absurd, unjust and inequitable. I wish the clergy would be quite frank with their congregations and reveal the whole facts. They have nothing to lose by so doing ; but they will and do lose a great deal, by virtually creating a cry of robbery and spoliation, and then engineering protests against a self- constituted cry. Sir, I very readily acknowledge the munificence of many clergy and others. I am aware that there are among them men who greatly value educa- tion, and would willingly place the best in the reach of the poorest child. I am aware that a few schools have been built by the generosity of private persons, and placed in trust for the "education of the poor In the principles of the Church of England." I know also that hundreds of Anglican schools could not have been built at all without the aid of Nonconformist

subscribers. I willingly acknowledge and bow before the sacrifice which these facts imply. I should like to know, however, wherein all these things beget a claim to the complete monopoly of elementary schools for denominational purnoses ? Now I don't care a single cent, whether the Govern- ment buys the schools, or rents them or throws them over and builds others. My own conviction is that it is legally and morally entitled to take them all and keep them in repair, pay every expense associated with them,and allow their free use for religious purposes to those who hold them now. Again, it is freely. stated that Nonconformists have not spent money qn education, therefore they have cared nothing for it. First, British schools and Wesleyan schools have arisen mainly to keep the children of Nonconformists away from the atmosphere of Roman Catholic and Anglican schools,and partly as a protest against the insufficient and inefficient education given in them. Generally speaking Nonconformists have always contended and willingly paid for a State system of schools. This has cost them far more than applying for State grants and building voluntary schools of their own, would have done, hence the origin of the late' Board School system in IS7Tand the support Free Churchmen have accorded it. Nonconformists havo seen the folly of multiplying small schools for sectarian purposes, nearly always understaffed, with the staff badly paid and the oft-times crushing " despotism " associated with the system. While, however, Anglicans and Raman Catholics have been applying lor State grants, Free Churchmen have been attending to their Sunday Schools, which have cost them 2 millions. They are the best equipped schools for religious teaching in the world, excepting perhaps those of the newer American type. Finally, neither Canon St evenson nor the clergy of his church, nor the Roman Catholic clergy, have pro- tested at all against the glaring injustice with which the Act of 1902-03 aims a deadly blow at the religious convictions of Free Churchmen. Little Churchmen and little Catholics seem to be synonymous in their minds with " Christian " ; and drilling the mind in orthodox theology—and very orthodox it is too—with religious training. So be it, but for such teaching no section of the Christian Church can be allowed to dip its hand in the public-purse. Public control must be absolute. Nobody must be penalised for his religion.— Yours &c., .101 IN FRANCIS MA'THEWS. Baptist Church, Latchford.

div.head: INFIRMARY.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY.
EXTENSION SCHEME SANCTIONED. -- 112,000 Required.

The rapidly increasing demands upon the accommoda- tion of the Infirmary have made an extension at an early date absolutely necessary, and at the annual meeting of the Governors of the Institution, held at the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon, a scheme which will involve an expenditure of between £lO,OOO and £12,000 was approved. The meeting, which was largely attended, was presided over by Mr. J. Charlton Parr. In the annual report, it was stated that there had been an increase of 65 in the number of patients treated in the House, the average number of beds occupied being the same as last year, viz. :-34, and the average estimated cost per bed was £5B 15s. Od., as against £62 14s. id. in the preceding year The ordinary income during the year had been £3,134. which was £l5 7s. 4d. less than last year, and the ordinary expenditure had been £3,108 12s. 10d., which was £lO3 4s. Bd. less than the previous year. The extraordinary expenditure had been the payment of balance of the account for the electric lift, viz., £47 Bs. 2d. The year began with a debit balance due to the expenditure and income account of £667 135., and it closed with a debit balance of £689 14s. The increase was owing to the payment out of Revenue account of the balance of the cost of the electric lift. In common with hospitals elsewhere,the Congregational collections showed a decrease, which was a matter of regret. The continued increase in the amount received from the Workingmen's Committtee was chiefly due to the larger number of systematic coltections from the works. The Board were glad to acknowledge this improvement and looked forward hopefully to still greater support from these collections. It had been felt for a considerable time that an extension of the Infirmary was called for by the increase of population in the town and district, and by the constantly growing number of applicants for treatment in the Institution. An Extension Committee appointed by the Board of Management had care- fully considered the matter,and with the concurrence of the Board, Messrs. W. and S. Owen had been consulted. They had prepared plans and estimates for the erection of a new Pavilion, with three floors, to accommodate 66 extra beds. Also it was proposed to erect a Nurses' Home for the Nursing Staff on ground adjoining the present buildings. It was estimated that the cost would be from £lO,OOO to £12,000. It should be stated that in 1900, some land and property in Beamont, Hendrick and Leigh streets were purchased by the trustees of the Infirmary with a view for future use for extension purposes. Part of this land and property, purchasd at £3,400, came within the scope of the projected exten- sion. It was obviously desirable that, through the generosity of the public in response to the proposed appeal, an equivalent amount might ultimately be replaced in the endowment fund. The board had very great pleasure in announcing the receipt of the under- mentioned donations towards the extension of the Infirmary :—The Hon. Ellinor Wilson-Patten,£los ; the Hon. Elisabeth Wilson-Patten £105; the Charity Lodge of Freemasons, £5 ss. The Board had to record with great regret the death of Mr. Thomas Birchall, who was for 28 years a member of the Board of Management, and for five years a member of the House Visitors and Finance Committee. They also greatly regretted the death of Mr. Peter Stubs,J.P., who was a life governor, and for 15 years a trustee of the Institution. The Medical Board in their report referred to the large increase of operations performed and also em- phasized the want of beds for medical cases, which at present had to be treated in their own homes—a most unsatisfactory and undesirable arrangement. There had been a decrease in the number of home patients, this being chiefly due to the absence of epidemics during the year and to an improvement in the condition of trade. The Board was strongly of opinion that there would be a considerable diminution in the number of home-patients and out-patients if the Dispensary were used only by proper persons for the receipt of charity, as there was no doubt that recommendations were pre- sented by persons who were well able to pay their own medical attendant. The reports were adopted. The election of officers resulted as follows : —Presi- dent, Mr. J. Charlton Parr ; hon. treasurer, Mr. George Dakin ; hon. auditor. Mr. C. Jackson Holmes ; hon. medical officers, Mr. E. A. Fox (consulting), Mr. G. W. Joseph. Mr. C. E. Richmond, Mr. Ernest E. Bowden; hon. assistant medical officers, Mr. R. Smith, Mr. E. J. Fox, Mr. G. H. Joseph ; Board or Management. the President and Vice-Presidents, and the Rev. Harry Vernon Pigot, M.A , Mr. Henry Thornton, Mr. J. Douglas Buckton, Mr. George Thompson, Rev. Father ;J. P. Whittle, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Mr. W. J. For- -1 shaw, Rev. William Bracecamp, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, Captain G.R.Crosfleld, Rev.C.H.Cook,Mr.John Roberts, Mr. Thomas Burton, Mr.C. M. Watkins, MrAV. Daintith, the members of the Medical Board, and the Hon. Treasurer. Votes of thanks were accorded to the officers and the various committes, special reference being made to the splendid services of the Workingmen's Committee. In an interesting and powerful speech the Hey. JOHN YONGE moved: "That this meeting of the Governors of the Infirmary is of opinion that the time has come for a considerable extension of the accommodation pro- vided. Plans have been furnished by Messrs. W. and , I S. Owen and approved by the Board of Management I whereby it is proposed to erect a pavilion having three 1 storeys, which would contain 66 beds, bringing the total ' accommodation up to 104. The plans also include a separate home for the nursing staff. This meeting I authorizes the Board of Management to place the matter before the public and invite for it a general and gener- I out support." The rev, gentleman pointed out that the first public function which he attended in Warrington was theopening of theinfirmary on January 24th,1877 by the / Right Hon. P.. A. Cross. at that period the population I of the borough was about 38,000 and the building which was inaugurated cost £8,122 and provided 23 beds. Ex: , tensions which had since been made brought the total number of beds to 40 which he considered was entirely ) inadequate to cope with the needs of the present popu- lation of nearly 70,000. He believed no place in Eng- land was so poorly provided with hospital accommoda- -1 tion in proportion to its population. The rev. gentleman referred to the great increase in the number of patients. ' Owing to the lack of accommodotion serious surgical cases had had to be refused, medical patients bad to be I turned out prematurely to create room for surgical cases, ' and a few weeks ago he believed there were nearly twenty cases waiting for places.Mr.Yeilge said the fear which some people expressed that sufficient fun& would not he forthcoming to erect the extension and provide ' for its upkeep was a slur on the generosity and humanity of Warrington people which they did not deserve. '1 Mr. W. P. RYLANDS seconded and pointed out that 1: large sums had recently been raised in other towns for , Infirmary extensions, including £20,000 at St. Helens, , and Warrington ought not to be behind. At present it , !stood at the bottom of the list of similar towns in , regard to the number of beds per thousand of the , population.

div.head: THROWING OFF THE INCUBUS.
div.p: THROWING OFF THE INCUBUS.
A WORD ON ENGLISH POLITICS.
[Bs, Mr. H. Whitham.]

At last the dear old tight little island has wakened up. The weight that has for so many years been pressing the life, the very manhood out of its people has been thrown on one side and it is now possible for the bold Briton to once more breath and think. What is the cause of this landslide ? The Tories have insisted that the real question before the nation was Home Rule. If we take them at their word, well, the nation has given its answer. But the Tory will make a sad mistake if he thinks the election has had but one, or even half-a-dozen Incubuses pressing him into the ranks of the unemployed. There is an unspeakable and altogether incomprehensible mortal who finds his home in the British Isles. He is known as the " Conservative workingman." He seems to believe in what John Morley calls " The sacred caste," that is, a party who, like the German war lord,s iule and govern by Divine right. In other words the Tory workingman has no confidence in his own powers of thought and is quite sure that if he were to act on his own powers of volition he would at once go straight to the dogs. Well, let us not say more about this timorous party just now. It has fox once ventured into fresh fields and pastures new, and if the party now in power do not make things hum, and teach the Tory workingman a lesson or two some of us will be deceived.

The discussion on Protection did not go just as I would have liked. The positions taken up by Mr. F. Monks and Mr. Gandy were tenable only as involv- ing the retaliatory spirit. This policy once adopted, with its consequences foreseen and acknowledged, it seems to me the positions taken by the two gentlemen were good. Tbe fight being over,and"C.-B." having a substantial majority behind him, what is the next move ? Of course the Tariff question, so far as the Government is concerned, is dead, yet not buried if Air. Chamber- lain remains true to his word, and I think he is likely to do that. The electors may not have voted on Home Rule, but they have most decidedly spoken out strong and straight on the Labour question It is not many years since crowds of unemployed paid a visit to the West End. There was quite a little bit of horse play, and it required considerable tact to prevent another Hyde Park episode. It should not be forgotten that Free Trade Hall, Manchester, stands on historical ground, and history has been known to repeat itself. While there can be no comparison made between England and Russia it must be acknow- ledged that at least in one respect there is a similarity of condition in the two countries that requires some attention. I refer to the insatiabla greed of the landowners. This same greed has grown in the United States to such glaring proportions that considerable uneasiness is seen throughout the country and it is felt something must be done, and soon, if a state of anarchy is to be avoided. There seems to be considerable fear lest the new blood now introduced into the House of Commons should ask for

too much, and John Morley has thought fit to give a reassuring word on this all important question. With respect to this bogey that Mr. Morley attempts to lay, it will be well to examine it and see what it really is. There is, year by year, a constantly increasing number of men and women drifting into the unem- ployed class, and every large town has its " east " end. The places those unfortunates crowd into cannot be called homes. The only parson you have in Warrington, the Rev. H. Dunnico said recently. " Every man had a right to a clean healthy, sanitary home. The house in which a man lived exercised a great influence over his character and because of that it was important that the influence should be an elevating one." Is there anything elevating, home-like or sanitary likely to influence for good the character of these growing thousands of unemployed? Not anything, and here is the real bogey. The wealthy, from Royalty down to the poorest sympathising mortal, may give, but it is all useless. It is the cause that must be got at, and if this cause is not reached very soon all the reassuring words that John Morley or anyone else can utter will not prevent a mighty uprising that will sweep before it all the vested interests man in his greed hugs to his poor mean soul. Look at Russia with its teeming millions robbed of every right. Its people driven to revolution, and murdered by the thousand, and the , rich, how do they spend their time and the people's ' earnings? Go over the European Continent and you find the idle rich Him-, the gambling hells and the health resorts while °the ranks of the unemployed grow, and the man who has work must be content to earn a four or live and twenty shillings a week and with this bring up a family in respectability. I see your Tory members are charging the working- men with ingratitude. What in the name of common sense have the labourites to be thankful for? Is it not time that the word Conservatism is but a euphemism for privilege and vested interest ? There is a spirit of movement in the air, and the nation that will not wake up and save itself from a worn out and effete policy must see itself eclipsed by the wide- awake ones. Measures that make millionaires, do not, even sometimes, add to the happiness of the millions. We have seen three hundred millions of pounds sterling spent and oceans of blood shed because Mr. Rhodes and Mr. Chamberlain were con- tent to be the puppets of the Park Lane millionaires. That war was said to be waged to find an outlet for white iabour. Yu have seen the Asiatic enslaved and made to add to the already bursting coffers of the Randlords, and what adds to the greater shame of all this, the native son of Africa is told to stand on one side as the digging of diamonds will not afford him a living wage. NOSY let us have a word about war. I often wonder if the workingman of whatever political party he may belong to, has ever read any of the fearful descrip- tions, that have in recent years been published, of what a battle field is like. Can any of us, reading of those scenes of horror, see with our minds eye all or a part of what it all means? Thihk of the desolate homes. Think ef the butchery going on within the hospitals and think of the cripples and incapables of all sorts and sizes 'that are now wandering on this earth w ith nothing but honour and patriotism to put in their empty stomachs. I yield to no one in love for my native land, but I don't want my share of it to be located in the Potter's Field. I don't want my love for my country to be worked upon by the "sacred caste." I tell my fellow-workmen that it is

as sure as we have to toil and moil day in and day out, this sacred caste foments wars, makes us workingmen of the various nations slay and murder one another. These idle rich seek the excitement of war. They muse and encourage glorious war. They anticipate coming back with honour, like conquering heroes, to their baronial halls. Some years ago a Member in the House of Commons shamelessly stated to his fellow-Members that there was nothing else but war and the Church for the younger sons of the rich to look to. I aril now reading John Morley's "Life of Gladstone"l (cheap edition). I wish every labourite would buy this and read it. Reading between the lines a little makes me more certain than ever I was before that Great Britain is made up of two nations, the " Haves" land the "Have nots."—they who live at the West End ' and the mobs that make up the East End. Mr. IMorley says writing of the period 1853 :—" The Whigs of this time were men of intellectual refine- ment ; they had a genuine regard for good govern- ' ment, and a decent faith in reform ; but when we chide the selfishness of machine, politicians hunting office in modern democracy, let us console ourselves s lby recalling the rapacity of our oligarchies." "It i melancholy !" muses Sir James Graham, "to see how little fitness for office is regarded on all sides' and how much the public employments are treated as booty to be divided among successful combatants." Again, coming down to our own day, we have in Winston Churchill's biography of his father, just issued, Lord Salisbury in the most cynical fashion drawing the veil from the Tory party, and showing its unblushing selfish face. Writing to Lord Randolph he says —" I think the classes %nd the dependents of class ' are the strongest ingredients in our composition, but we have so to conduct our legislation that we shall give some satisfaction to both classes and masses. This is specially difficult with the classes —because all legislation is rather unwelcome to them, as tending to disturb a state of things with which they are satisfied. Evidence in abundance is to hand showing and proving beyond any doubt, and this proof comes from the" sacred caste' itself, that selfishness and indiffer- ence have been the chief characteristics of the govern- ing classes in their treatment of the toiling masses, and yet they have had, entirely in their own hands, full control of the army and navy, to force us out to shed the blood of our fellow workers, and also,at their

own good pleasure to declare war: Justia Mc earthy in his history of the reign of Queen Anne says —in speaking of the war with Spain in I 700.—" In j fact, the war, like most wars in those times. was made in the interests of princes and dynasties only, and had as little to do with the condition and the sympathies of the population of Spain as with those of the popula- tion of England." I think we ask nothing but what is reasonable of ! our conservative fellow workman that now he has ! put his hand to the progressive plough he shall keep it , there. We have had proof in abundance that there is plenty of Conservatism in the British workingman. Tell, the Radicals will join with him in conserving ! all our fathers have sent down to us that is worth conserving. Don't expect too much from the new Government, remember the House of Lords is neither ended or mended yet, and while you have John Burns in the Cabinet you have the " sacred caste " also well represented in the aristocratic Whig families. John has already bundled out of place, one of these idle j place seekers, who thought it right to draw his salary and give nothing in return, and more may follow. I Remember, the problem of civilization to-day is, how to ' eliminate the parasite. There is a ! certain amount of work to do in the world. ! ! Somebody has got to work. The reason some people have to work from daylight .to dark, and their work is never done, is because some people never work at all. I speak feelingly. on this question. Here am I fast getting on for seventy, and I and the crowd along with me, and let j me say all the rest of this crowd of young men, forced J to make SI hours a week, and not one of us dare pro- j test against it. The unemployed question is the most I burning one of the day. We have just perfected an I elevating machine with which a dozen men will accomplish what it has hitherto taken 400 men to do, and so the ranks of the unemployed are swollen. Day by day invention and discovery aided by greed add to the strenuousness of life. In America, and I under- stand it is much the same in F4urope, the company work for will not engage a new man if lie is over thirty-five, and one of the consequences of all this is, that every day, sure, we have the record of one or more lives gone out, and the poor suicide leaving behind I him a written statement, "Life is too much, I quit." j The skilled workman and the common labourer so' far have been the victims of the vicious system under which we exist. Now comes in the small tradesman. ' Mr. Marshall Field, whose death is just reported, was placed by Mr. Stead first among the gods constituting " the Chicagoan Trinity," his fellow-deities being Philip D. Armour and George M. Pullman. One of the most striking passages in Mr. Stead's book about the Windy City is that in which he depicts the ruin wrought among small tradesmen by the building up of Mr. Field's mammoth store. He quotes old resi- dents as telling him how when each fresh department was added it was as if a cyclone had gone forth among the smaller houses in the same line of business. The new department would be opened and carried on at "out rates" until all competitors had been driven out, Mr. Field contentino himself meanwhile with the profit of the other departments. Men who had busi- nesses of their own in retail stores by which they expected to make a living and presently retire with a competence were thus compelled to put up their shutters. Those who know Chicago can testify that this picture is by no means overdrawn. This man gathered in twenty-five million dollars and said it was his. He is gone and I wonder what his reception will be on the other side if Jesus Christ is his judge. Now the trouble seems to be that few men can seek their own advancement without injuring someone else. The workman tries through his Union to improve his con- ditions. He meets with protest. He looks to Socialism,and this is voted ridiculous. If he looks to co-operation the small tradesman cries out he is being ruined. The fact is that only the prosperous, the minority, who are anxious to let th ings alone, say "this is the best of all possible worlds." Now, I should be very sorry if my readers should think I wish to encourage class hatred. No, I am anxious that the worker, he who has hitherto been known as the " Conservative workingman ", should help me to get away from the past and all its bad and wretched institutions. I want you to disestablish the Church, and give every minister of religion to under- ! stand that he must do his part to make this world worth living in. I want our friends to help the world's socialists to fling out the curse of war, and let us have the brains that are now devoted to the making of war material turned to constructive work. I want them to help us to make the land as free as the air we breathe or the sun that gives us warmth.l want them to help us to build up a leisured class that is not an idle class ; to put into force the old law that if a man does not work neither shall he eat. lam not a Christian man but that is no reason why I should not ask my Christian friends to help rue to put the Sermon on the Mount and a few more of the scripture sayiuga into the way of doing some good practical work. 'lf the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, let us give it to Him, and then He will perhaps give some of we landless ones, a little more than what we require to cover us. I noticed in a London despatch that Lady Strathcona and Mountroyal, wife of the Canadian High Commissioner, has donated 52,500d015. to Queen Alexandra's fund for the assistance of the unemployed. In accordance with a stipulation of the donor, 47,000d015. of the amount will be expended in providing for the emigratioa to Canada of deserving workmen and their families. This set me thinking and the result may be seen in my next. H. WILITHAM, Feb. 14th, DOG.

would put their hand to the plough and sweeping aside the cringing counsels of the timorous and the fatal philosophy of the egotist work through and by means of the League for the security and prosperity of our great Empire. A considerable discussion followed, the proposal largely on the ground that a national citizen army was unnecessary and that a voluntary army was preferable. Captain.CrosUeld was heartily thanked for his paper and it was decided to arrange an evening upon which he could address the Association in reply to the criticism which had been passed upon his address. At the meeting on Monday night the Rev. J. E. Matthews will deliver an address on "The new factor in British politics."

div.head: PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE.
div.p: PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE.
VISLT OF MR. A. H. CROSFIEI,D, M.F. Labour Questions and Social Reforms.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., had an extremely enthusiastic reception on Moe.day evening when he addressed a meeting of the Progressive Labour League—a flourish- ing organization which did a great deal to bring about the magnificent victory at the recent election. The meeting was held at the Liberal Club, Mr. Thomas Barnes presiding. In the course of his address the CHAIRMAN said the greatest credit for that organization was due to their esteemed friend Mr. Howes. When it was formed apathy prevailed in regard to Liberal politics, but an uphill task was splendidly accomplished and victory was achieved. (Applause.) It had been stated that the league was formed with the one object of assisting the return of Mr. Crosfield. That was not so. for while the election of their member was one of the main purposes, the League existed to undertake propaganda work—to educate the people as to the evils which they suffered under the Conservative Government, Mr. Crosfield was I the best standard bearer that Liberalism in Warrington I ever had. Notwithstanding the great defeat at the 1900 I election he was ready to respond to the first call of , duty. (Applause.) Mr. Barnes concluded by moving I the following resolution : "That this meeting of the Warrington Progressive Labour League offers to Mr. A. H. Crosfleld its hearty congratulations on his recent great victor y_in wrenching the Parliamentary repre- sentation of Warrington from the party of retrogression by whom it has been so long held, and rejoices that he has been privileged to carry the mandate of the borough to swell the great majority by which Sir Henry Campbell-Banuerman's Government is sup- ported in keeping intact the Free Trade principles— the bulwark of the nation's prosperity—assures him of its entire confidence in his furthering of measures of reform tending to the welfare of the labouring classes of this country and wishes him a long life of service in Parliament." (Applause.) Mr. E. WYNNE-JONES seconded. For twenty years, he said, Liberalism had waited for that great victory. The day of their deliverance had arrived and all were glad that the thraldom of Toryism had been overthrown. He believed it had been overthrown once and for all and that the Tory party would never regain the ascend- ancy in Warrington. They were proud of their Mem- ber and believed his heart had been touched with the needs of democracy. He bore an honoured name. The late Mr. John Crosfleld was always in the forefront of the battle against intolerance and injustice of eery kind and they were glad to know that Mr. Arthur Crosfield was following in his father's footsteps. He held up the flag of Liberalism when the faint- hearted ones were leaving the old ship to take care of itself. They were proud of his past and had every confidence in his future. They believed that in the wide field which he had enteredhe would accomplish , great things that would be a credit to himself and to the town he represented. The Government now in power meant business. He (Mr. Jones) believed the Government would give them a national system of education, efficient and free from any poison of sectarian bias, that they would give food for the hungry children and do something for the housing of the poor and for the eeneral welfare of the nation. They rejoiced in the victory in Warrington because they had helped to swell the Liberal majority which he believed had already killed Protection and would do something to avenge the past wrongs of Tory legislation. (Applause.) Mr. J. ELWELL supported, and described Mr. C rosfleld's victory as a workingmen's victory. They had bethought put back the protective policy of the late Government for twenty, thirty, or forty years. The present Govern- ment had gone a step forward with regard to old-age pensions. Workingmen produced the wealth of the nation, and they had a right to ask for 'pensions as well as soldiers, sailors, policemen and others who had positions under the Government. Probably during the next few years they would- have a practical scheme brought forward. Mr. J. WILLETT and Mr. THOMAS SMITH also sup- ported the resolution, the latter remarking that he felt sure that on any trade union question Mr. Crosfield would act satisfactorily. The resolution was passed with cordiality. Mr. CROSFIELD, who was warmly cheered on rising to reply, said that although it was only a few weeks since he went to the Mother of Parliaments and it was therefore a little early in the day to render any account of one's stewardship (he did not think they had sent for him for that purpose yet) still the House of Commons—this first great Democratic Parliament which had been sent there,differentlfrom any other Parliament that had gone before—was so chock full of ideas and energy and one heard so much of the great legislative programme that was ahead of them, that he assured them he felt in this dilemma: that he would like either to stop there and talk into the middle of next week or to keep silence for about twelve months till he had been able to digest not the general principles—because his mine was made IT on them long since—but more of the details, of the FAR REACHING REFORMS which were calculated to bring great and permanent bene- fit to the whole of the masses of this nation. (Applause.) When one considered the work that lay before Parba- NATIONAL MILITARY SERVICE. ment and the earnestness of the men who had to carry it out,.he thought they would understand how very , --- enter himself the Captain Crosfield Addresses the impressive it was to a new-corner like h the House ond see the splendid spirit that animated Progressive side, and the grand way in n yhie h the Junior Liberals. ordinary Liberal and the more distinctive Labour hm e m , ----- b neithere r s werea reactionary absolutely House joouisnei nogf Lords hands, or a ny other determined tat body, , A well attended meeting of the Warrington Junior nor any undue selfishness of capitalistic instinct, should Liberal Association was held at Gregory's Cafe on prevent any single reform that was for the good of the Monday evening, at which an address on National people being carried. (Applause.) As to the, remarks Service was delivered by Captain Crosfield, Mr. E. of Mr. Smith, it was kind of him to repose confidence Osborne presided. in him (Mr. Crosfield), although he happened to be in a During the course of his address Captain Crostield small way a bit of a capitalist—(applause)—and some sa id.that the preparation for war, especially where that people thought it was easier for a camel to get through preparation was spread over the shoulders of the whole the eye of a needle than for a capitalist to do his nation, prevented war, and it was therefore the duty of duty in Parliament. He had not we were remiss in this respect for we had no adequate noticed any tendency on the part of Liberals in the second line of defence. To talk of the navy as being all House, whether capitalists or not, to throw cold water sufficient for protecting our shores was perniciously on the great measures which he could only allude to unsound. These surely were motives the Protective system was like the old man of the sea strong enough to "prick us to redress " and he was 1 who got his arms round the workingman's neck, because sure that those really convinced by what he had said 1
775-14th St. San Francisco.

every employer of labour could come and say "If you take off these duties my trade which depends on Protection will be gdne and out you go." That was what was hampering the democratic party of America to-day. The democrats of America stood for Free Trade but the Republican interest had got that threat banging over the heads of the people which enabled them to block the way towards Free Trade. The greatest curse of all in America was the fact that by the system of Protection they had made the rich richer, and bad increased those diversities of conditions of life which it was the object of the Liberal party through wiser legislation and juster taxation to reduce in our own country. They had heard a great deal about

THE ENING OE' THE iENDULIIM. The distinguished member for a Midland constituency said he would give the Government two years' office, but it was only a few nights since he (Mr. Crosfield) heard the leader of the Opposition say they would probably have six. (Laughter.) There were, however, judges in very high positions on the Conservative side who said that the Progressive party had come to stay for a great deal more than six years, and it was, said Mr. Crosfield, most necessary that they should do so. They heard people making slighting remarks about democracy, and comparing the wave of democratic opinion in England with what happened in the olden. times. They said: "Democracies : What have they always been? Something to be flattered and amused, They are unstable, unreliable." There was, however this glorious difference—that in the old days of the old civilizations the democracy were not educated. It was just because we had got education and that fairy god- mother of mankind, science, leading us on to better ideals and more widespread knowledge that we were , going to build our civilization on a sound basis. They were hopeful that the day would never come when the traveller from New Zealand, in Macaulay's picturesque phrase, would sit on the steps of Westminster Bridge sketching the ruins of the once-existing Houses of Par- liament. (Applause.) He (Mr. Crosfield) was sitting in the House the other day on one of the back benches which was close to the distinguished strangers' gallery and he supposed there was a very distinguished stranger just behind him. Several progressive measures were being discussed on the Address, including payment of members, graduated taxation of large incomes to find a means for the payment to members of reasonable salaries which ought to be paid certainly to all Labour members but which it was better and more dignified to offer—although that might sound a little self-interested —to all members, leaving those who chose to refuse them to do so. In addition they had ventured to lay their hands on the Ark of the Covenant and propose the taxation of site values which the Conservatives did not like but which would be a God-send to the country, not only as a means of raising revenue, but of bettering the cond;tions of the dwellers in the towns. He had heard one or two members of the Conservative Benches speak of the " revolution " that was on the tapis and he supposed this rather frightened the dis- tinguished friend sitting behind him, for he heard a gloomy " Ah : spoliation in the air !" (Laugh- ter.) Members were not allowed to discuss matters over the rail with any strangers, but he felt inclined to tell his friend to make his mind easy as it was

NOT SPOLIATION EUT JUSTICE. (Applause.) He (Mr. Crosfield) had never on any plat- form said, and he was not going to say now, that he thought by any device of Parliament they could manage to make every man in the country equal, and he did not think whether their respective holding be very small or large they wanted to hand it all over to anybody, however well chosen they might be, to take charge of. Neither did he think those who were married wanted their wives to be instructed as to whether their herrings were to be boiled or fried. (Laughter). What he would say was that they were not afraid of any so-called Socialistic measures, provided that they were intended to give a better chance and fairer opportunity to the individual all through the land, to whatever class he might happen to belong. Some of these measures hada Socialistic look about them. There was no word that conveyed a greater range of meanings than Socialism. Sir William Harcourt not long before he died said we were all becoming Socialists now. He (Mr. Crosfield) had never chosen to use the word himself, because he thought it was misunderstood, and he did not want to profess any- thing that he was notkeen to fight for. He did not, however, intend to quarrel with friends of his who liked to use the word as applied to some of those measures which, after all, from his point of view were directed towards the better kind of individualism which gave each man the fairest chance and the fullest opportunity. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfield briefly explained the circumstances under which he " paired " on the occasion of the Chinese Labour vote. He said that while personalities might be useful in certain quarters, where Tory measures had for long enough been at a discount under the late Government, and where it was not convenient to criticise Liberal measures now, one might be excused in the future from discussing personal matters with the newspaper critic to whom he alluded when explicit statements made twice over in the Press were not accepted. He advised his friends present to take cani gran() sails—and with a very big pinch of salt too— further statements from the same quarter. Continuing,he said,he would do his utmost to do Justice to the trust they had reposed in him. There was only one time in the year while the House was sitting that he would like to be away for two or three weeks, and he would tell them why. He did not go in for shooting, fishing, hunting and so on,but he had got a weakness.(Laughter).Some of the English papers had said he had done something to spread what was called International golf. He had been elected president of a Golfing Association in Switzer- land. Ho helped them to introduce the game into Paris and he had arranged inter-club matches between England and Cannes, which took place just before Easter. If it was required of him he would be willing to give up the two or three weeks which were necessary for the pur- pose, but he told them frankly he would be sorry if they insisted on his doing so. They had heard a great deal about games in England being overdone, and he knew too much attention was paid to the sporting papers and tips. The promiscuous and eternal betting was also a bad thing. At the same time we in England had a great deal of the fighting spirit in us and he hoped we always would have. Within reasonable limits he hoped a fair share of that fight- ing spirit would find vent in the channels which Mr. Haldane was going to give them plenty of opportunity for as he (Mr. Crostield) knew from conversations he had recently had with him. For his own !kart, however he did not wish to see all that fighting spirit find its outlet in military channels. He would rather the good old English love of games was maintained. He hoped they would not think he was a very hopeless backslider for having enjoyed the pastime of golf and encouraged it to some extent. At any rate, he did not think they would find him a backslider in politics because he was ( proud not merely to follow in the footsteps of his father and grandfather but to go onward in the march of progress. (Applause.) He repudiated alto- gether the insinuations that one heard about spoliation and that kind of thing. They did not bear unkindly feelings towards anyone, but they were determined that unjust privilege should not prevent their going forward. They would act, in the splendid words of that great man in America of our own race—Abraham Lincoln— " with malice to none ; with charity to all." They had a great work to perform for the nation and for the whole world, because they had the best chance and opportunity for developing the peoßle, and raising before them higher ideals as time went on. They would carry out that work without fear and with confidence and they would do it for the permanence, honour and glory of the Empire. (Applause). The Rev,H. DUNNICO, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and to Mr. Crosfield said he was quite convinced that no question affecting the interests of workingmen would not receive the same careful con- sideration and generous treatment from Mr. Crosdeld as from any Labour member. The working men of this country had beendeluded and tyrannised over long 'enough. Now they were thinking for themselves, and were being educated, which accounted for the great, turnover in public opinion at the last election. He din not think there,ever was a greater opportunity for the party than there was to-day. Never was there such an atmosphere in the House of Commons ; never was there such a rugged, genuine Prime Minister as Sir Henry Campboll-Bannerman. He believed Mr. Crosfield had the necessary qualifications for becoming a minister of this country, and hoped that at some future time he would have the honour of being in the Cabinet. (Applause.) Mr. ErAvELL seconded the vote, and said be under- stood one of the first things Mr. Crosfield did when he entered the House was to promise to support the grant- ing of a day to the Labour party in order that the Trades Disputes Bill might be introduced. The vote was heartily accorded and Mr. Crosfield briefly responded and said he should endeavour to fairly represent all classes in the constituency.

A recent school examination elicited the following definitions: "Noah's wife," wrote one boy, "was called Joan of Arc." "Water," wrote another, "is composed of two gases, oxygen and cambrigen." " Lava," replied a third youth, "is what the barber puts on your face." "A blizzard," insisted another child, "is the inside of a fowl." Truly a little know- ledge is a very dangerous thing—even with children. —" Tatler."

Warrington Trades and Labour Council. The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held at the 80ld-street schools on Tuesday. —A lengthy discussion arose upon the report by Mr. Higginbottom, delegate to the Warrington L.R.C., who said that he had given notice that at the next meeting of the Committee he would move " That any candidate willfully making a misstatement should bear the whole of the expense incurred by his candidature." Several delegates were of opinion that I the resolution was hardly severe enough and it was pro- posed to add that any candidate guilty of such conduct be not again allowe.d to stand in labour interests." Upon a Tote being taken it wal decided ti allow Mr. Higgin- bottom to adhere to his original resolution.—The question of the painting of the markets was also considered. It was urged by the painters delegate that after the first fortnight of the workmen who registered themselves at the labour bureau as out of work, in the great majority of cases non-union men, were given the preference over trade unionists who were out of work but who had not registered their names. Councillor Stott pointed out that the trade union. rate of wages was being paid, and upon his agreeing to supply the council with further particulars as to the cost of the work itc.,the subject was allowed to drop.

An inquest was held at Warrington on Wednesday on the body of Charles Henry Osborne, aged two, scn of a pit labourer, residing at a, Hoyle-street, who died on Sunday night at the Infirmary as the result of severe burns.—The evidence showed that the deceased went upstairs, and a few minutes later screams were beard, and on the mother rushing upstairs the child was found to be enveloped in flames. There was no fire in the room, but the child had some matches in its hand, and it was evident they had been struck.—A verdict of " Accidental death was returned. LAWN MOWERS, Garden Rollers, Garden Tools, Lawn Mower repairs a speciality.—J. S. GARLAND, 51,Bridge at,, Warrington.—Advt. Mr A. Chamberlain to Visit Warrington. At a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of Conservative Workingmen held in Manchester on Saturday, the secretary announced that, in compliance with their decision to invite Mr. Austen Chamberlain, M.P., as a principal speaker at their next annual conference, the right hon. gentleman had consented to attend,and had fixed the 19th of May as a convenient date. Alderman Bennett said he was pleased, on behalf of the Warrington Executive, to invite the conference to that town. The invitation was cordially accepted by the Federation Committee. The Polyglot Society. At the last meeting, the topic" Die Kiinstliche Darstellung der Textiltasern : eine Gross-Industrie der Zukunft ? " " The artificial production of textile fibres: a great industry of th future ? " was intro- duced by Mr. E. C. Kayser. In his paper, Mr.Kayser asked what will be the results if science succeeds in supplanting natural products by artificial ones ? and he dealt with, among other things, the Chardonnet, and like processes of silk manufacture, showing spedimens of such artificial silks. Some of those present, after hearing the paper read, thought that the future of British industry was threatened,and a strong wish was expressed that the lecture be given before a general audience. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Man's Enormous Heart. Coroner Brighouse held an inquest at Warrington on Wednesdity afternoon on the body of William Haslam, aged thirty, son of John Haslam, of 9i Leicester-street, who suddenly expired whilst at work in the benzine department of Messrs. Crosfield's soap- works on Monday. The father said that his son had complained of feeling dizzy through the fumes at the works.—Dr. Smith who made a post-mortem examina- tion, certified that the man's heart weighed 14oz. instead of Boz., the normal weight. There were other traces of heart disease. He was of the opinion that the fumes did not accelerate his death. Owing to the condition of the heart death might have occurred at any time.—A, verdict of " Death from natural causes" was returned. Co-operative Employees' Concert. The Co-operative Employees Glee Society held their first annual concert in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, on Tuesday evening, and the event proved a gratifying success. The glee party, under the able conductorship of Mr. A. E. Trow, rendered the choruses and part songs Sailors? Chorus," " When the Swallows,' " Celmrades of Hope " and " Soldiers' farewell " in taste and expression and were heartily encored for their interpretation of the stirring " Com- rades' song of hope." The following artistes also con- tributed to an excellent programme : —Miss Jennie Jones (soprano)' Miss Lily Fairhurst (contralto), Mr. J, Willett (tenor), Mr. R. Rushton (bass), and Mr. S. Hardman (concertina solo),Mr. E. R. Ford (harp solo). and Mr. Arthur Bearle (humorist). Both vocalists and instrumentalists acquitted themselves most creditably and encores were frequent. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASb MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Band of Hope Concert. A very successsul concert, promoted by the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Band of Hope, was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. There was a large attendance, Mrs. Moores presiding and delivering a I short address. An admirable programme was sub- mitted, and all the items were well received. Miss Oakley and Mr. E. G. Rickers gave two pianoforte duets in a creditable manner. Songs were well ren- dered by Miss Hipkiss and Mr. 11. Plumpton ; and violin solos by Master Sidney Boswell proved popular features. There were also interesting recitations by Miss M. Pitt, Alice Tindall, Annie Sankey and Emily Barnard, and other highly successfnl items were an action song by Elsie Whitfield and Dolly Caine; a dialogue by Lily Turner and Fred Payne, and a musical sketch " Factosy Lassies " by L. Oakley, L. Owen, M. Thomas, and D. Martin. Humorous songs and recitations were given by Mr. D. Sutton, of Ashton-in-Makerfield, and created considerable amuse- ment. Mr. E. G. [tickers ably discharged the duties of accompanist. A. hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the arsistes, on the proposition of Mr. W. Wilkes seconded by Mr. J. Corradine, UNDER TIIE CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt. The National Union of Teachers. The thirty-seventh annual conference of the National Union of Teachers is to be held in Scar- borough during Easter week. The gathering will commence on April 12th but the Conference proper will open at 10.30 a.m. on Monday April 16th and close on the following Thursday. The chair-will be taken by Mr. I'. P. Sykes, the president elect, of the Great Horton Council School, Bradford, from whom a presidential address dealing powerfully with current educational questions may be expected. An important programme of motions on educational subjects will be discused. It is anticipated that over 2,000 members will be present as the appointed representatives of the 480 branches of the Union. It is expected that deputations of teachers from Scotland, Ireland, 'Belgium, France, Holland, Switzerland, and of delegates from the Teachers' Guild of Great Britain and Ireland, the Association of Head Teachers, and the Cc-operative Union, will also attend the Confer- ence, The following have been appointed as delegates to represent the Warrington Branch of the Teachers' Union: —Miss Brookes, Mrs. Stansfield, and Messrs. J. Upson, J. Cann, J. Wright, J. Stansfield, S. Jeffery and W. Wilcock-son.
